problems.title: Inertia tensor of three unequal point masses
problems.objective: Build the inertia tensor of three unequal axial point masses and use its anisotropy to predict angular momentum and rotational energy for a nonprincipal spin.
problems.statement: Three point masses are fixed at positions measured from an origin: mass $m$ at $(a,0,0)$, mass $2m$ at $(0,a,0)$, and mass $3m$ at $(0,0,a)$. Construct the full inertia tensor about the origin. For angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega(1,1,1)$, compute $\mathbf L$ and the rotational kinetic energy. State the dimensions.
permittedResults: For point masses, $I_{ij}=\sum_k m_k(r_k^2\delta_{ij}-r_{k,i}r_{k,j})$.
$T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Add the tensor contribution of each mass rather than treating the three distances as one scalar moment. Next: Multiply the diagonal tensor by the stated angular-velocity vector, then use $T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L/2$. Finally: Check positivity and the units of every resulting quantity.
hints: Add the tensor contribution of each mass rather than treating the three distances as one scalar moment.
Multiply the diagonal tensor by the stated angular-velocity vector, then use $T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L/2$.
Check positivity and the units of every resulting quantity.
problems.solution: Each mass on a coordinate axis contributes only to the two transverse diagonal entries. Therefore $\mathbf I=ma^2\operatorname{diag}(5,4,3)$. Hence $\mathbf L=ma^2\Omega(5,4,3)$ and $T=\tfrac12ma^2\Omega^2(5+4+3)=6ma^2\Omega^2$. Tensor entries have units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, angular momentum has $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, and energy has joules. The tensor is positive definite, as expected because the masses do not all lie on one line through the origin.
rubricCriteria: The three point-mass contributions sum to $ma^2\operatorname{diag}(5,4,3)$ with vanishing off-diagonal entries.
Tensor multiplication gives $\mathbf L=ma^2\Omega(5,4,3)$ and the half-dot-product gives $T=6ma^2\Omega^2$.
Mass-moment, angular-momentum, and energy units are correct, and positive definiteness is connected to the noncollinear mass placement.

commonErrors.description: Uses $I=\sum m_kr_k^2$ as one scalar for an arbitrary rotation axis.
commonErrors.consequence: A scalar moment erases directional inertia and produces the wrong angular momentum vector for the stated spin.

commonErrors.description: Computes $T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L$ without the factor one half.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing the one-half factor doubles the kinetic energy while leaving the independently computed angular momentum unchanged.

problems.flawedProof: The total scalar moment is $6ma^2$, so the inertia tensor is $6ma^2\mathbf 1$ and the energy is $18ma^2\Omega^2$.

problems.title: Tensor parallel-axis shift for a displaced ring
problems.objective: Extend the parallel-axis theorem to a rank-two inertia tensor and evaluate the displaced-ring tensor with both center-of-mass cross terms justified.
problems.statement: A thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ lies in the $xy$ plane with center $C$. Its central inertia tensor is $\mathbf I_C=\operatorname{diag}(MR^2/2,MR^2/2,MR^2)$. A new origin $O$ is displaced from $C$ by $\mathbf d=d\mathbf e_x$. Derive the tensor parallel-axis theorem from the defining mass integral and calculate $\mathbf I_O$. Check the limits $d=0$ and $R=0$.
permittedResults: Use $\mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_C+M(d^2\mathbf 1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T})$ only after deriving the vanishing center-of-mass cross terms.
problems.strategy: First: Expand the tensor integrand after writing each position relative to the displaced origin. Next: Use the center-of-mass condition to remove both cross terms and then evaluate the rank-one shift. Finally: Recover both the unshifted ring and point-mass limits.
hints: Expand the tensor integrand after writing each position relative to the displaced origin.
Use the center-of-mass condition to remove both cross terms and then evaluate the rank-one shift.
Recover both the unshifted ring and point-mass limits.
problems.solution: Write a material point as $\mathbf r_O=\mathbf r_C+\mathbf d$ and expand $r_O^2\mathbf1-\mathbf r_O\mathbf r_O^{\mathsf T}$. The terms linear in $\mathbf r_C$ integrate to zero because $C$ is the center of mass. Thus $\mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_C+M(d^2\mathbf1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{diag}(MR^2/2,M(R^2/2+d^2),M(R^2+d^2))$. At $d=0$ the central tensor returns. At $R=0$ this is the tensor of a point mass a distance $d$ along $x$, namely $M\operatorname{diag}(0,d^2,d^2)$.
rubricCriteria: Expansion of the defining integral identifies the two linear terms and removes them using the center-of-mass condition.
The displacement along $x$ leaves $I_{xx}$ unchanged while adding $Md^2$ to the two transverse moments.
Both $d=0$ and $R=0$ recover the central ring and displaced point-mass tensors, respectively.

commonErrors.description: Adds $Md^2$ to all three principal moments, including the moment about the displacement axis.
commonErrors.consequence: An isotropic shift incorrectly adds inertia about the displacement axis, where the offset has zero lever arm.

commonErrors.description: Invokes the scalar parallel-axis theorem without showing why tensor cross terms vanish.
commonErrors.consequence: Without the center-of-mass cancellation, the tensor theorem is asserted only for this ring rather than demonstrated generally.

problems.flawedProof: The shift is isotropic, so $\mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_C+Md^2\mathbf1$; all three diagonal entries increase equally.

problems.title: Principal axes of a coupled planar inertia tensor
problems.objective: Diagonalize a planar inertia tensor with a product-of-inertia term and explain the geometric freedom created by its repeated principal moment.
problems.statement: A rigid body has inertia tensor $\mathbf I=I_0\begin{pmatrix}4&-\sqrt3&0\\-\sqrt3&2&0\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}$ in an orthonormal body basis. Find all principal moments and an orthonormal principal-axis basis. Identify any degeneracy and explain the resulting freedom of principal axes.
permittedResults: A real symmetric inertia tensor has an orthonormal eigenbasis.
problems.strategy: First: Diagonalize the symmetric planar block and keep the already decoupled $z$ direction. Next: Normalize the eigenvectors and compare the planar eigenvalue with the third diagonal entry. Finally: Verify orthogonality and explain the continuous freedom within a degenerate eigenspace.
hints: Diagonalize the symmetric planar block and keep the already decoupled $z$ direction.
Normalize the eigenvectors and compare the planar eigenvalue with the third diagonal entry.
Verify orthogonality and explain the continuous freedom within a degenerate eigenspace.
problems.solution: The planar block has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-6\lambda+5$, so its dimensionless eigenvalues are $1$ and $5$. For $\lambda=1$, an eigenvector is $(1,\sqrt3,0)/2$. For the planar $\lambda=5$, an eigenvector is $(\sqrt3,-1,0)/2$. The $z$ axis also has eigenvalue $5$. Thus the moments are $I_0,5I_0,5I_0$. The first axis is unique up to sign; every orthonormal pair spanning the plane perpendicular to it is a valid pair of principal axes for the doubly degenerate moment. Direct substitution verifies each eigenpair.
rubricCriteria: The planar characteristic polynomial yields eigenvalues $1$ and $5$, not the displayed diagonal entries.
The normalized planar eigenvectors and the $z$ axis form an orthonormal eigenbasis with moments $I_0,5I_0,5I_0$.
The two-dimensional repeated eigenspace is recognized as allowing arbitrary orthonormal principal-axis pairs within it.

commonErrors.description: Reads the diagonal entries $4I_0,2I_0,5I_0$ as the principal moments despite the product of inertia.
commonErrors.consequence: Reading diagonal entries as eigenvalues ignores coupling and gives incorrect principal moments and axes.

commonErrors.description: Finds the repeated moment but still claims its two principal axes are unique.
commonErrors.consequence: Claiming uniqueness inside a degenerate eigenspace discards the continuous family of equally valid principal directions.

problems.flawedProof: The coordinate axes are already principal because the matrix is symmetric; the principal moments are its three diagonal entries.

problems.title: Rotational energy on an inertia ellipsoid
problems.objective: Compare pure principal-axis rotations at fixed angular momentum and separate that variational problem from the superficially similar fixed-angular-speed comparison.
problems.statement: A torque-free body has principal moments $I_1=2I_0$, $I_2=3I_0$, and $I_3=5I_0$. For a fixed angular-momentum magnitude $L$, compute the rotational energy for pure rotation about each principal axis. Determine which axis minimizes and which maximizes energy. Refute the claim that the largest moment produces the largest energy at fixed $L$.
permittedResults: For principal-axis rotation at fixed $L$, $T=L^2/(2I_i)$.
problems.strategy: First: State explicitly that angular momentum, not angular speed, is held fixed. Next: Evaluate $L^2/(2I_i)$ for all three axes and order the results. Finally: Contrast the fixed-$L$ calculation with the fixed-$\omega$ calculation.
hints: State explicitly that angular momentum, not angular speed, is held fixed.
Evaluate $L^2/(2I_i)$ for all three axes and order the results.
Contrast the fixed-$L$ calculation with the fixed-$\omega$ calculation.
problems.solution: The three energies are $L^2/(4I_0)$, $L^2/(6I_0)$, and $L^2/(10I_0)$. Thus the largest moment $I_3$ minimizes energy, while the smallest moment $I_1$ maximizes it. The alleged monotonicity is reversed because fixing $L$ forces $\omega=L/I_i$. At fixed angular speed the ordering would instead follow $T=I_i\omega^2/2$; mixing the two constraints causes the false claim.
rubricCriteria: Each energy is evaluated as $L^2/(2I_i)$ under the explicitly fixed-$L$ condition.
The smallest moment is correctly identified as the energy maximum and the largest moment as the minimum.
The response explains why fixing angular speed reverses the ordering and cannot be substituted mid-comparison.

commonErrors.description: Uses $T=I_iL^2/2$ and therefore makes energy grow with the moment.
commonErrors.consequence: Multiplying by inertia instead of dividing reverses the fixed-angular-momentum energy ordering.

commonErrors.description: Changes from fixed angular momentum to fixed angular speed while comparing axes.
commonErrors.consequence: Switching the held quantity changes the optimization problem, so the resulting axis ranking does not answer the question.

problems.flawedProof: Because $T=I\omega^2/2$, the $I_3$ rotation has the largest energy even though the problem fixes $L$.

problems.title: Misalignment of angular velocity and angular momentum
problems.objective: Quantify the misalignment of angular velocity and angular momentum in an anisotropic body and verify it against the rotational-energy identity.
problems.statement: In principal coordinates let $\mathbf I=I_0\operatorname{diag}(1,2,4)$ and $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega(1,1,0)$. Find $\mathbf L$, the angle $\alpha$ between $\mathbf L$ and $\boldsymbol\omega$, and the kinetic energy. Check that $2T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L$.
permittedResults: $\mathbf L=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\cos\alpha=(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L)/(|\boldsymbol\omega||\mathbf L|)$.
problems.strategy: First: Apply the tensor componentwise in the principal basis. Next: Use the dot-product definition of the angle without assuming the two vectors are parallel. Finally: Verify the energy identity and state the alignment condition.
hints: Apply the tensor componentwise in the principal basis.
Use the dot-product definition of the angle without assuming the two vectors are parallel.
Verify the energy identity and state the alignment condition.
problems.solution: $\mathbf L=I_0\Omega(1,2,0)$. The dot product is $3I_0\Omega^2$, while the magnitudes are $\sqrt2\Omega$ and $\sqrt5I_0\Omega$. Hence $\cos\alpha=3/\sqrt{10}$ and $\alpha\approx18.4^\circ$. The energy is $T=3I_0\Omega^2/2$, so $2T=3I_0\Omega^2=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L$. Alignment would occur only along a principal axis or within a degenerate principal subspace.
rubricCriteria: Applying the diagonal tensor produces $\mathbf L=I_0\Omega(1,2,0)$ rather than a scalar multiple with one common moment.
Normalized dot products give $\cos\alpha=3/\sqrt{10}$ and the reported angle near $18.4^\circ$.
The kinetic energy satisfies $2T=\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L$ and the alignment condition is stated correctly.

commonErrors.description: Sets $\mathbf L=I_0\boldsymbol\omega$ as though the body were spherical.
commonErrors.consequence: Replacing the tensor by $I_0$ falsely forces parallel vectors and loses the anisotropic energy contribution.

commonErrors.description: Computes the angle from component ratios without normalizing both vectors.
commonErrors.consequence: An unnormalized component ratio is not a cosine and can report an angle inconsistent with the vector dot product.

problems.flawedProof: Angular momentum is always parallel to angular velocity, so $\alpha=0$ and $T=I_0\Omega^2$.

problems.title: Angular velocity from 3-1-3 Euler-angle rates
problems.objective: Evaluate body angular velocity from a declared 3-1-3 Euler convention while keeping the three instantaneous rotation axes distinct.
problems.statement: Use the active $3$-$1$-$3$ Euler convention $R=R_z(\phi)R_x(\theta)R_z(\psi)$. The body components are $\omega_1=\dot\phi\sin\theta\sin\psi+\dot\theta\cos\psi$, $\omega_2=\dot\phi\sin\theta\cos\psi-\dot\theta\sin\psi$, and $\omega_3=\dot\phi\cos\theta+\dot\psi$. Evaluate $\boldsymbol\omega$ when $\theta=\pi/3$, $\psi=0$, $\dot\phi=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\dot\theta=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\dot\psi=-1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Explain why adding the three rates as scalars is invalid.
permittedResults: Use the supplied convention-specific component formulas.
problems.strategy: First: Fix the stated Euler convention before substituting rates. Next: Evaluate each body component with the correct trigonometric factor. Finally: Check the angular-speed units and distinguish rotations about different axes.
hints: Fix the stated Euler convention before substituting rates.
Evaluate each body component with the correct trigonometric factor.
Check the angular-speed units and distinguish rotations about different axes.
problems.solution: Substitution gives $\omega_1=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\omega_2=2\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\omega_3=2\cos(\pi/3)-1=0$. Therefore $\boldsymbol\omega=(1,\sqrt3,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ in body components and $|\boldsymbol\omega|=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The Euler rotations occur about different instantaneous axes, so their signed rates cannot be added as collinear scalars.
rubricCriteria: Substitution into the supplied convention gives body components $(1,\sqrt3,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The component norm is $2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, with the cancellation in the third component shown explicitly.
The explanation ties scalar-rate addition failure to rotations about different moving axes, not to arithmetic alone.

commonErrors.description: Adds the rates to obtain a single angular speed $2\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ along the body $z$ axis.
commonErrors.consequence: Adding Euler rates as collinear scalars assigns the correct magnitude to the wrong spatial direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses formulas from a different Euler-angle ordering without transforming the convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Mixing Euler orderings changes component signs and axes, so subsequent attitude kinematics use an incompatible convention.

problems.flawedProof: The three rates sum to $2\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so the vector is $(0,0,2)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Body-frame kinetic energy of an asymmetric rotor
problems.objective: Partition angular momentum and energy among the principal components of a measured asymmetric-rotor state.
problems.statement: A body has principal moments $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(0.20,0.30,0.50)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and instantaneous body angular velocity $(3.0,-2.0,4.0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Compute the angular momentum components, total rotational kinetic energy, and the fraction of that energy in the third component.
permittedResults: In principal axes, $L_i=I_i\omega_i$ and $T=\sum_i I_i\omega_i^2/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Multiply each angular-velocity component by its matching principal moment. Next: Sum one half of $I_i\omega_i^2$ rather than squaring angular-momentum components directly. Finally: Check the dot-product identity and normalize the requested energy fraction.
hints: Multiply each angular-velocity component by its matching principal moment.
Sum one half of $I_i\omega_i^2$ rather than squaring angular-momentum components directly.
Check the dot-product identity and normalize the requested energy fraction.
problems.solution: $\mathbf L=(0.60,-0.60,2.00)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. The component energies are $0.90$ J, $0.60$ J, and $4.00$ J, giving $T=5.50$ J. The third component contains $4.00/5.50=8/11\approx72.7\%$ of the energy. The dot-product check gives $\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L=11.0$ J, twice the kinetic energy.
rubricCriteria: Componentwise multiplication gives angular momentum $(0.60,-0.60,2.00)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
All three quadratic energy contributions are nonnegative and sum to $5.50$ J.
The third-axis fraction is $8/11$ and the dot-product check returns twice the total energy.

commonErrors.description: Uses one averaged moment for every component.
commonErrors.consequence: Averaging the moments destroys the measured componentwise angular momentum and shifts every energy contribution.

commonErrors.description: Drops the square on a signed angular-velocity component and obtains negative energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Letting a signed angular velocity create negative quadratic energy violates positive definiteness of rotational kinetic energy.

problems.flawedProof: Use the averaged moment $\bar I=(0.20+0.30+0.50)/3$ for every axis. Then $\mathbf L=\bar I\boldsymbol\omega$ and $T=\bar I(3^2+(-2)^2+4^2)/2=4.83$ J.

problems.title: Transforming a body-fixed torque into space
problems.objective: Transform a short body-fixed thruster torque into space coordinates and integrate it over a frozen-attitude burn.
problems.statement: At an instant the body-to-space attitude is a rotation by $30^\circ$ about the common $z$ axis. A thruster supplies body torque $\boldsymbol\tau_b=(12.0,0,0)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Find the space components $\boldsymbol\tau_s$. If it acts for $0.250\,\mathrm s$ while attitude change is negligible, find the space angular impulse.
permittedResults: A physical vector transforms as $\boldsymbol\tau_s=R_z(30^\circ)\boldsymbol\tau_b$.
problems.strategy: First: Write the declared body-to-space rotation matrix. Next: Rotate the torque before integrating it over the short interval. Finally: Verify that the rotation preserves magnitude and attach angular-impulse units.
hints: Write the declared body-to-space rotation matrix.
Rotate the torque before integrating it over the short interval.
Verify that the rotation preserves magnitude and attach angular-impulse units.
problems.solution: $\boldsymbol\tau_s=(12\cos30^\circ,12\sin30^\circ,0)=(6\sqrt3,6,0)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. The angular impulse is $\Delta\mathbf L_s=\boldsymbol\tau_s\Delta t=(1.5\sqrt3,1.5,0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. Its magnitude is $3.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, equal to $|\boldsymbol\tau_b|\Delta t$, confirming norm preservation by the rotation.
rubricCriteria: The active $30^\circ$ rotation sends the body torque to $(6\sqrt3,6,0)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ in space.
Multiplication by $0.250$ s yields the stated angular-impulse vector with consistent SI units.
Norm preservation verifies both the rotation direction and the impulse magnitude of $3.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.

commonErrors.description: Treats body components as space components despite the nonzero attitude angle.
commonErrors.consequence: Leaving body components unchanged predicts angular momentum delivery along the wrong inertial direction.

commonErrors.description: Rotates by the negative angle without changing the declared active convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the inverse rotation reverses the transverse impulse and conflicts with the declared active attitude map.

problems.flawedProof: The torque is $(12,0,0)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ in every frame, so the impulse is $(3,0,0)$ in space.

problems.title: Euler equations and an instantaneous acceleration audit
problems.objective: Recover Euler's principal-axis equations from the transport theorem and use them to compute an instantaneous torque-free angular acceleration.
problems.statement: Derive Euler's equations in principal body axes from $\boldsymbol\tau=(d\mathbf L/dt)_{space}$ and the rotating-basis derivative rule. Then take $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(2,3,5)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\boldsymbol\omega=(1,2,3)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and zero torque. Compute $(\dot\omega_1,\dot\omega_2,\dot\omega_3)$ at that instant.
permittedResults: For a body-frame vector, $(d\mathbf L/dt)_{space}=(d\mathbf L/dt)_{body}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$.
problems.strategy: First: Relate the space derivative to the body derivative before inserting principal-axis components. Next: Expand $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$ with a consistent cyclic sign convention. Finally: Evaluate the three derivatives and verify instantaneous energy conservation.
hints: Relate the space derivative to the body derivative before inserting principal-axis components.
Expand $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$ with a consistent cyclic sign convention.
Evaluate the three derivatives and verify instantaneous energy conservation.
problems.solution: With $L_i=I_i\omega_i$, the derivative rule gives $I_1\dot\omega_1+(I_3-I_2)\omega_2\omega_3=\tau_1$, $I_2\dot\omega_2+(I_1-I_3)\omega_3\omega_1=\tau_2$, and $I_3\dot\omega_3+(I_2-I_1)\omega_1\omega_2=\tau_3$. Equivalently for zero torque, $I_1\dot\omega_1=(I_2-I_3)\omega_2\omega_3$, and cyclically. The values are $\dot\omega_1=-6.0\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $\dot\omega_2=3.0\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, and $\dot\omega_3=-0.400\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Substitution into $dT/dt=\sum I_i\omega_i\dot\omega_i$ gives zero, an energy check.
rubricCriteria: The space derivative is decomposed into a body derivative plus $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$ before components are taken.
Cyclic moment differences yield $(-6.0,3.0,-0.400)\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ for the supplied state.
Direct substitution into $dT/dt$ cancels to zero, independently checking all three signs.

commonErrors.description: Sets body-frame $\dot{\mathbf L}$ equal to space torque and omits $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$.
commonErrors.consequence: Omitting the transport term makes torque-free body components constant and erases real Euler-top motion.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same moment difference sign in all three cyclic equations.
commonErrors.consequence: A noncyclic sign pattern prevents the energy cancellation and violates torque-free conservation.

problems.flawedProof: Torque-free motion makes every body component of angular velocity constant, so all three derivatives vanish.

problems.title: Free precession of a symmetric top in body axes
problems.objective: Solve finite-amplitude symmetric-top motion exactly and relate body-frame component precession to the distinct space-frame precession of the symmetry axis.
problems.statement: A torque-free symmetric top has $I_1=I_2=I$, $I_3=2I$, and finite initial body components $\omega_1(0)=\epsilon$, $\omega_2(0)=0$, $\omega_3(0)=\Omega$. Solve Euler's equations exactly for all three components. Then find the fixed angular-momentum magnitude, the oriented angle between the symmetry axis and $\mathbf L$, and the space-frame precession rate of that axis. Distinguish body and space precession and check the spherical limit $I_3\to I$.
permittedResults: For a symmetric top, $\omega_3$ is constant and $\omega_1+i\omega_2$ obeys a first-order complex equation.
problems.strategy: First: Use axial symmetry to isolate the constant axial component and solve the transverse Euler pair exactly. Next: Compute $\mathbf L$ in body components and derive the space motion of the symmetry axis from $d\mathbf e_3/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf e_3$. Finally: Separate the two precession rates and verify the spherical-rotor limit without assuming a small transverse component.
hints: Use axial symmetry to isolate the constant axial component and solve the transverse Euler pair exactly.
Compute $\mathbf L$ in body components and derive the space motion of the symmetry axis from $d\mathbf e_3/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf e_3$.
Separate the two precession rates and verify the spherical-rotor limit without assuming a small transverse component.
problems.solution: Euler's third equation gives $\dot\omega_3=0$. The first two give $\dot\omega_1=-[(I_3-I)/I]\Omega\omega_2$ and $\dot\omega_2=[(I_3-I)/I]\Omega\omega_1$. Thus $\omega_1+i\omega_2=\epsilon e^{i\Omega_b t}$ with $\Omega_b=(I_3-I)\Omega/I$. For $I_3=2I$, $\omega_1=\epsilon\cos\Omega t$, $\omega_2=\epsilon\sin\Omega t$, and $\omega_3=\Omega$ exactly, without a small-$\epsilon$ approximation. Also $L=I\sqrt{\epsilon^2+4\Omega^2}$ and $\cos\beta=2\Omega/\sqrt{\epsilon^2+4\Omega^2}$. Since $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf L/I-(I_3/I-1)\Omega\mathbf e_3$, $d\mathbf e_3/dt=(\mathbf L/I)\times\mathbf e_3$: the symmetry axis precesses in space about fixed $\mathbf L$ at rate $\Omega_s=L/I=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+4\Omega^2}$, distinct from $\Omega_b$. As $I_3\to I$, $\Omega_b\to0$ and the body components become constant, while the spherical body's marked axis still rotates kinematically about $\mathbf L$ unless aligned.
rubricCriteria: The transverse Euler pair gives $\omega_1+i\omega_2=\epsilon e^{i\Omega_b t}$ while $\omega_3$ remains constant.
For $I_3=2I$, the fixed angular momentum and oriented cone angle follow from $L=I\sqrt{\epsilon^2+4\Omega^2}$.
The identity $d\mathbf e_3/dt=(\mathbf L/I)\times\mathbf e_3$ yields the space rate and the spherical limit is interpreted without a small-$\epsilon$ assumption.

commonErrors.description: Uses the space precession rate as though it were the body-component precession rate.
commonErrors.consequence: Substituting the space cone rate for the body component rate confuses two different rotations and changes the predicted attitude.

commonErrors.description: Lets $\omega_3$ vary even though the third Euler equation vanishes.
commonErrors.consequence: Allowing the axial component to vary contradicts the exactly vanishing third Euler equation for an axisymmetric body.

problems.flawedProof: All components rotate at $2\Omega$ because the axial moment is twice the transverse moment.

problems.title: Energy and angular-momentum invariants of the Euler top
problems.objective: Prove both Euler-top quadratic invariants by explicit cyclic cancellation rather than by invoking conservation slogans.
problems.statement: For a torque-free triaxial body, prove directly from Euler's equations that $2T=I_1\omega_1^2+I_2\omega_2^2+I_3\omega_3^2$ and $L^2=I_1^2\omega_1^2+I_2^2\omega_2^2+I_3^2\omega_3^2$ are conserved. Do not appeal only to a verbal conservation law.
permittedResults: Use the cyclic zero-torque Euler equations and display the cancellation of the cubic product.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate each quadratic invariant explicitly. Next: Insert all three Euler equations and collect the common product $\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3$. Finally: Show the moment-difference coefficients vanish and check dimensions.
hints: Differentiate each quadratic invariant explicitly.
Insert all three Euler equations and collect the common product $\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3$.
Show the moment-difference coefficients vanish and check dimensions.
problems.solution: Differentiating gives $\dot{(2T)}=2\sum I_i\omega_i\dot\omega_i$. Replacing each $I_i\dot\omega_i$ by the corresponding moment difference times the product of the other two components makes the coefficient of $2\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3$ equal $(I_2-I_3)+(I_3-I_1)+(I_1-I_2)=0$. Similarly, $\dot L^2=2\sum I_i\omega_i(I_i\dot\omega_i)$ has coefficient $I_1(I_2-I_3)+I_2(I_3-I_1)+I_3(I_1-I_2)=0$. Both invariants are therefore constant. Their dimensions are energy and squared angular momentum, respectively.
rubricCriteria: Differentiation of $2T$ produces one cubic product whose three moment-difference coefficients sum to zero.
The corresponding weighted cancellation for $L^2$ is displayed with the additional factors of $I_i$.
The two conserved quantities are distinguished dimensionally as energy and squared angular momentum.

commonErrors.description: Claims each term in the differentiated sums vanishes separately.
commonErrors.consequence: Termwise vanishing is false for generic torque-free motion; only the cyclic sum conserves energy.

commonErrors.description: Uses conservation of $\mathbf L$ in space to assert that every body component $L_i$ is constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Space-fixed angular momentum can have time-varying body components, so componentwise constancy is not a valid proof.

problems.flawedProof: Since torque is zero, $\dot\omega_i=0$ for each component, which proves both invariants without any cancellation.

problems.title: Stability frequencies about the extreme principal axes
problems.objective: Linearize torque-free rotation about both extreme principal axes and compare their moment-dependent transverse frequencies.
problems.statement: Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$. Linearize the torque-free Euler equations about steady rotations $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_1$ and $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_3$. Derive the two small-perturbation frequencies. Evaluate them for $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)I_0$.
permittedResults: Retain only terms linear in the two transverse perturbations.
problems.strategy: First: Perturb only the two components transverse to each steady principal-axis rotation. Next: Eliminate one transverse component to obtain a second-order equation and preserve every moment-difference sign. Finally: Evaluate the positive squared frequencies for the stated moments.
hints: Perturb only the two components transverse to each steady principal-axis rotation.
Eliminate one transverse component to obtain a second-order equation and preserve every moment-difference sign.
Evaluate the positive squared frequencies for the stated moments.
problems.solution:
About axis 1, the transverse equations combine to $\ddot u_2+\Omega^2[(I_3-I_1)(I_2-I_1)/(I_2I_3)]u_2=0$, so $
u_1=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_3-I_1)(I_2-I_1)/(I_2I_3)}$. About axis 3, $
u_3=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_3-I_1)(I_3-I_2)/(I_1I_2)}$. Both squared frequencies are positive. For moments $(1,2,3)I_0$, $
u_1=|\Omega|/\sqrt3$ and $
u_3=|\Omega|$. This checks stability about both extreme axes without implying stability about the intermediate axis.
rubricCriteria: Only transverse first-order perturbations are retained about each steady spin.
The two squared frequencies contain the correct paired moment differences and positive denominators.
For moments $(1,2,3)I_0$, the results reduce to $|\Omega|/\sqrt3$ and $|\Omega|$ without making a claim about axis 2.

commonErrors.description: Replaces all moment differences by absolute values before deriving the linearized equations.
commonErrors.consequence: Premature absolute values erase the sign structure that distinguishes elliptic and hyperbolic perturbations.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that positivity for the two extreme axes also proves intermediate-axis stability.
commonErrors.consequence: Stability at the minimum and maximum moments gives no basis for classifying the intermediate-axis equilibrium.

problems.flawedProof: Replace every principal-moment difference by its absolute value before linearizing. The transverse equations then reduce to $\ddot u+\Omega^2u=0$ about either extreme axis, so both frequencies are $|\Omega|$.

problems.title: Two branches of steady heavy-top precession
problems.objective: Find both exact steady-precession branches of a heavy symmetric top and identify the discriminant separating allowed constant-tilt motion from nutation.
problems.statement: A symmetric top with fixed point has transverse moment $I_1$, axial moment $I_3$, center-of-mass distance $\ell$, and axial body component $\omega_3$. Take gravitational potential $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$. For constant nonvertical tilt $\theta$ and steady precession $\dot\phi=\Omega_p$, derive the quadratic condition for $\Omega_p$. For $I_1=0.200\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $I_3=0.100\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\omega_3=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $Mg\ell=0.500\,\mathrm J$, and $\theta=60^\circ$, calculate both branches.
permittedResults: Use the $\theta$ Euler-Lagrange equation with $\dot\theta=0$ and $\omega_3=\dot\psi+\Omega_p\cos\theta$.
problems.strategy: First: Write the heavy-top Lagrangian in the declared potential convention. Next: Set the nutation rate and acceleration to zero while retaining the coupling through $\omega_3$. Finally: Solve both quadratic roots and check the discriminant and torque dimensions.
hints: Write the heavy-top Lagrangian in the declared potential convention.
Set the nutation rate and acceleration to zero while retaining the coupling through $\omega_3$.
Solve both quadratic roots and check the discriminant and torque dimensions.
problems.solution: The constant-tilt equation is $I_1\Omega_p^2\cos\theta-I_3\omega_3\Omega_p+Mg\ell=0$. Numerically it is $0.100\Omega_p^2-1.00\Omega_p+0.500=0$, so $\Omega_p=5(1\pm\sqrt{0.8})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, or approximately $0.528$ and $9.47\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. These are the slow and fast precession branches. The discriminant condition $(I_3\omega_3)^2\ge4I_1Mg\ell\cos\theta$ is satisfied. Each term in the quadratic has units of torque.
rubricCriteria: The constant-tilt Euler-Lagrange equation retains inertial, gyroscopic, and gravitational torque terms.
Solving the resulting quadratic gives the slow and fast rates near $0.528$ and $9.47\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The discriminant and units of every term are checked under the stated potential convention.

commonErrors.description: Drops the $I_1\Omega_p^2\cos\theta$ term and therefore finds only one precession branch.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping the quadratic inertial term collapses two physical precession branches into an approximation valid only in a restricted regime.

commonErrors.description: Uses the opposite gravity sign without changing the declared potential convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the gravity sign moves the stationary condition to a different orientation convention and invalidates the numerical roots.

problems.flawedProof: Steady precession always has the single rate $Mg\ell/(I_3\omega_3)=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Nutation effective potential of a symmetric top
problems.objective: Reduce heavy-top nutation to a one-dimensional energy problem using its two cyclic momenta and expose the polar centrifugal barrier.
problems.statement: For the heavy symmetric top with $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$, eliminate the cyclic rates using $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$ and $p_\phi=I_1\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta$. Derive the one-dimensional nutation energy and its effective potential. Evaluate the effective potential at $\theta=\pi/2$ for $I_1=1$, $I_3=1/2$, $p_\phi=2$, $p_\psi=1$, and $Mg\ell=1/2$ in consistent units.
permittedResults: Solve first for $\dot\phi$ and use energy rather than substituting into the Lagrangian with the wrong sign.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the two conserved-momentum relations for the cyclic rates. Next: Insert the rates into the conserved energy and isolate the positive nutation kinetic term. Finally: Evaluate the stated angle and interpret turning points and polar barriers.
hints: Solve the two conserved-momentum relations for the cyclic rates.
Insert the rates into the conserved energy and isolate the positive nutation kinetic term.
Evaluate the stated angle and interpret turning points and polar barriers.
problems.solution: Elimination gives $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$. The energy becomes $E=I_1\dot\theta^2/2+U_{eff}(\theta)$ with $U_{eff}=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I_1\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$. At $\theta=\pi/2$, this is $4/2+1/(1)+0=3$ in energy units. Nutation turning points satisfy $E=U_{eff}$; the centrifugal denominator also shows why generic nonzero momenta prevent the symmetry axis from reaching $\theta=0$ or $\pi$.
rubricCriteria: The cyclic relations are inverted to give $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$.
The effective potential contains the squared momentum combination, the axial constant, and the declared gravity term with correct signs.
Its value at $\pi/2$ is three energy units, and turning points and polar exclusions follow from the same expression.

commonErrors.description: Forms an effective potential by substituting cyclic rates directly into the Lagrangian without a Routh or energy construction.
commonErrors.consequence: Naive substitution into the Lagrangian gives the wrong reduced sign structure because cyclic elimination is a partial Legendre problem.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor $\sin^2\theta$ and loses the polar barrier.
commonErrors.consequence: Removing $\sin^2\theta$ eliminates the coordinate barrier and permits generically impossible passage through the Euler poles.

problems.flawedProof: The effective potential is simply $Mg\ell\cos\theta$, so its value at $\pi/2$ is zero.

problems.title: Rolling disk on a circular track without slip
problems.objective: Enforce no slip for an upright disk following a horizontal circle and separate axle spin from vertical yaw in both contact kinematics and energy.
problems.statement: A thin disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rolls upright without slip while its center follows a horizontal circle of radius $\rho$ at constant speed $v$. The disk plane is tangent to the circle. Decompose its angular velocity into axle spin and vertical yaw, prove the instantaneous contact point has zero velocity, and derive the kinetic energy. Evaluate $|\boldsymbol\omega|$ and $T$ for $M=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=0.300\,\mathrm m$, $\rho=1.20\,\mathrm m$, and $v=1.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
permittedResults: For a thin disk, the axle moment is $MR^2/2$ and any diameter moment is $MR^2/4$.
problems.strategy: First: Resolve spin and yaw about their distinct instantaneous axes. Next: Apply $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/C}$ at the contact point. Finally: Use the correct principal moment for each component and check the straight-track limit.
hints: Resolve spin and yaw about their distinct instantaneous axes.
Apply $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/C}$ at the contact point.
Use the correct principal moment for each component and check the straight-track limit.
problems.solution: Choose $\mathbf e_\theta$ along the center velocity, $\mathbf e_r$ outward, and $\mathbf e_z$ upward. No slip requires axle spin $\boldsymbol\omega_s=-(v/R)\mathbf e_r$ because $\boldsymbol\omega_s\times(-R\mathbf e_z)=-v\mathbf e_\theta$. The disk also yaws with $\boldsymbol\omega_y=(v/\rho)\mathbf e_z$; this contributes no contact velocity because it is parallel to the center-to-contact vector. Thus $|\boldsymbol\omega|=v\sqrt{R^{-2}+\rho^{-2}}=5.154\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The energy is $T=Mv^2/2+(MR^2/2)(v/R)^2/2+(MR^2/4)(v/\rho)^2/2=3Mv^2/4+MR^2v^2/(8\rho^2)=3.410\,\mathrm J$. The straight-track limit $\rho\to\infty$ removes yaw energy.
rubricCriteria: The axle component cancels center velocity at contact while the yaw component is shown to contribute no contact velocity.
Spin and yaw use their distinct principal moments in the rotational-energy sum.
The numerical angular speed and $3.410$ J energy agree with the straight-track limit as $\rho$ grows.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $v=R|\boldsymbol\omega|$ on the total angular speed and therefore counts yaw as rolling spin.
commonErrors.consequence: Applying $v=R|\boldsymbol\omega|$ to yaw as well as axle spin imposes a false no-slip constraint.

commonErrors.description: Uses the axle moment for the vertical yaw component.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the axle moment for vertical yaw overcounts the yaw energy by a factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: The yaw rate also makes the contact point move, so no slip requires $v=R(v/R+v/\rho)$ and is impossible for finite $\rho$.

problems.title: A rolling sphere on a translating incline
problems.objective: Predict rolling-sphere motion relative to a horizontally accelerating incline, including pseudo-force, normal reaction, friction feasibility, and the equilibrium acceleration.
problems.statement: An incline descends to the right at angle $\alpha$ while translating to the right with constant acceleration $A$. In the nonrotating frame attached to the incline, a homogeneous sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rolls without slip; $I=2MR^2/5$. Derive its acceleration relative to the incline, the signed static friction, the normal force, and the minimum coefficient of static friction. Identify the acceleration $A$ that holds the sphere at relative equilibrium. Evaluate for $M=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=0.200\,\mathrm m$, $\alpha=30.0^\circ$, $A=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
permittedResults: Include the uniform pseudo-force $-MA\mathbf e_x$; with downslope positive its tangential component is $-MA\cos\alpha$ and its inward-normal component is $MA\sin\alpha$.
problems.strategy: First: Resolve gravity and the translational pseudo-force along and normal to the moving incline. Next: Combine signed translation, torque, and rolling constraint equations for the sphere. Finally: Audit force directions, the equilibrium acceleration, SI values, and the fixed-incline limit.
hints: Resolve gravity and the translational pseudo-force along and normal to the moving incline.
Combine signed translation, torque, and rolling constraint equations for the sphere.
Audit force directions, the equilibrium acceleration, SI values, and the fixed-incline limit.
problems.solution: Let $g_s=g\sin\alpha-A\cos\alpha$ be the signed effective downslope acceleration. Translation and rotation give $M a_{rel}=Mg_s-f$ and $fR=I a_{rel}/R$, so $a_{rel}=5g_s/7$. For $g_s>0$, $f=(2/7)Mg_s$ acts upslope; both signs reverse when $g_s<0$. Normal balance gives $N=M(g\cos\alpha+A\sin\alpha)$, hence $\mu_s\ge(2/7)|g_s|/(g\cos\alpha+A\sin\alpha)$. Relative equilibrium occurs at $A=g\tan\alpha$. Numerically $g_s=3.173\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $a_{rel}=2.266\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downslope, $|\dot\omega|=a_{rel}/R=11.33\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $f=2.72\,\mathrm N$ upslope, $N=28.49\,\mathrm N$, and $\mu_{s,min}=0.0955$. At $A=0$ the fixed-incline result returns.
rubricCriteria: Tangential projection produces the signed effective drive $g\sin\alpha-A\cos\alpha$ in the translating frame.
Translation, torque, and rolling give $a_{rel}=5g_s/7$ with friction direction tied to the sign of $g_s$.
The normal pseudo-force contribution leads to the reported force values, threshold $\mu_s$, and $A=g\tan\alpha$ equilibrium.

commonErrors.description: Omits the pseudo-force and obtains the ordinary fixed-incline acceleration independent of $A$.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring frame acceleration misses both the tunable tangential drive and the possibility of relative equilibrium.

commonErrors.description: Uses $N=Mg\cos\alpha$ even though horizontal frame acceleration has a normal component.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the fixed-incline normal force understates contact loading and produces the wrong no-slip coefficient.

problems.flawedProof: Because the incline translates without rotating, its acceleration cannot affect the sphere's motion relative to the incline.

problems.title: Center of percussion cancels the pivot impulse
problems.objective: Derive the center-of-percussion distance from coupled linear and angular impulse balances and verify the result for a uniform rod.
problems.statement: A planar rigid body is pinned at $O$, with center of mass a distance $d$ from the pin and moment of inertia $I_O$ about it. Starting from rest, it receives a transverse impulse $J$ at a point a distance $b$ from $O$ along the line from $O$ to the center of mass. Let the pin's transverse impulse be $R$, positive in the direction of $J$. Derive $R(b)$ and the center-of-percussion distance for which $R=0$. Then take a uniform rod of mass $M=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and length $L=1.20\,\mathrm m$, pinned at one end, with $J=9.00\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Find the required strike distance, angular speed, center-of-mass speed, kinetic energy, and an impulse-work check.
permittedResults: For an impulse of negligible duration, gravity contributes negligible impulse while the ideal pin fixes point $O$.
problems.strategy: First: Write angular impulse about the pin and linear impulse for the center of mass. Next: Eliminate the post-impact velocities using rigid-body kinematics and set the pin impulse to zero. Finally: Evaluate the uniform-rod case and close it with an energy-versus-impulse-work check.
hints: Take angular impulse about $O$, where the ideal pin impulse has zero moment.
Use $v_C=\omega d$ only after relating $I_O\omega$ to $Jb$.
At the center of percussion, compare $T$ with one half of $J$ times the final velocity of the struck point.
problems.solution: Angular impulse about $O$ gives $I_O\omega=Jb$. Linear impulse gives $Mv_C=J+R$, while rigid-body kinematics gives $v_C=\omega d$. Hence $R=J(Mdb/I_O-1)$, so $R=0$ at $b_{cp}=I_O/(Md)$. For a uniform rod pinned at an end, $d=L/2$ and $I_O=ML^2/3$, so $b_{cp}=2L/3=0.800\,\mathrm m$ and $I_O=1.44\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. Thus $\omega=Jb/I_O=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $v_C=\omega L/2=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and indeed $R=Mv_C-J=0$. The kinetic energy is $T=I_O\omega^2/2=18.0\,\mathrm J$. The struck point ends at speed $v_P=\omega b=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the linear impulsive-response check $Jv_P/2=18.0\,\mathrm J$ agrees.
rubricCriteria: Angular and linear impulse balances are combined with $v_C=\omega d$ to obtain $R=J(Mdb/I_O-1)$.
Setting $R=0$ gives $b_{cp}=I_O/(Md)$ and the uniform-rod value $0.800$ m with $\omega=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The center-of-mass speed, zero pin impulse, $18.0$ J kinetic energy, and impulse-work check are mutually consistent.

commonErrors.description: Uses the center-of-mass inertia $I_C$ in the angular impulse equation about the pin.
commonErrors.consequence: Replacing $I_O$ by $I_C$ predicts the false rod result $b=L/6$ and fails to cancel the pin impulse.

commonErrors.description: Treats the struck point as a particle of mass $M$ and omits the body's rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: Using only $J/M$ cannot enforce both rigid-body kinematics and angular impulse, so it misses the center-of-percussion condition.

problems.flawedProof: Take moments about the pin but use $I_C=ML^2/12$. Then $I_C\omega=Jb$ and $Mv_C=J$ give $b=I_C/[M(L/2)]=L/6$, so the center of percussion lies near the pin.

problems.title: A reaction wheel slews its spacecraft without external torque
problems.objective: Use angular-momentum exchange to relate spacecraft attitude to a reaction wheel's relative rotation and audit the coupled kinetic energy.
problems.statement: An axisymmetric spacecraft bus has moment of inertia $I_b$ about its slew axis, excluding a coaxial reaction wheel of inertia $I_w$. Let $\theta$ be the bus angle and $\phi$ the wheel angle relative to the bus, so the wheel's inertial angular speed is $\dot\theta+\dot\phi$. The system starts from rest and experiences no external torque. Derive the zero-angular-momentum relation, the bus attitude change caused by a relative wheel turn, and the kinetic energy during a constant-rate coast. For $I_b=900\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $I_w=100\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, a rest-to-rest wheel turn $\Delta\phi=5\pi\,\mathrm{rad}$, and a coast rate $\dot\phi=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find $\Delta\theta$, both inertial angular speeds during the coast, the total kinetic energy, and the internal angular impulse accumulated during spin-up.
permittedResults: The wheel's inertial rate is the sum of the bus rate and its rate relative to the bus.
problems.strategy: First: Write total angular momentum using the wheel's inertial, not relative, rate. Next: impose its conserved zero value and integrate the rate relation for the attitude change. Finally: evaluate both bodies' kinetic energies and the equal-and-opposite spin-up angular impulses.
hints: The wheel contributes $I_w(\dot\theta+\dot\phi)$ to inertial angular momentum.
Because the proportional rate relation holds throughout the maneuver, integrate it over the relative wheel turn.
Compute the wheel energy using $\dot\theta+\dot\phi$ and verify it with the reduced inertia.
problems.solution: The conserved angular momentum is $L=I_b\dot\theta+I_w(\dot\theta+\dot\phi)=(I_b+I_w)\dot\theta+I_w\dot\phi=0$. Therefore $\dot\theta=-I_w\dot\phi/(I_b+I_w)$ and $\Delta\theta=-I_w\Delta\phi/(I_b+I_w)=-\pi/2=-90.0^\circ$. During the stated coast, $\dot\theta=-2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and the wheel's inertial rate is $18.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The energy is $T=I_b\dot\theta^2/2+I_w(\dot\theta+\dot\phi)^2/2=1.80\times10^4\,\mathrm J$, agreeing with $T=[I_bI_w/(I_b+I_w)]\dot\phi^2/2$ and reduced inertia $90.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. Spin-up changes the wheel angular momentum by $I_w(18.0)=1.80\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m\,s}$ and the bus by the equal-and-opposite amount; their sum remains zero.
rubricCriteria: Total inertial angular momentum is written as $(I_b+I_w)\dot\theta+I_w\dot\phi$ and set to its initial zero value.
The integrated relation gives $\Delta\theta=-\pi/2$, while the coast rates are $-2.00$ and $18.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for bus and wheel inertially.
Direct and reduced-inertia energy calculations agree at $1.80\times10^4$ J, and the spin-up impulses are equal and opposite.

commonErrors.description: Writes $I_b\dot\theta+I_w\dot\phi=0$ and omits the bus contribution to the wheel's inertial rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting denominator $I_b$ instead of $I_b+I_w$ overpredicts the slew and violates the declared relative-angle convention.

commonErrors.description: Calls $\dot\phi$ the wheel's inertial rate and uses it directly in the wheel energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring the bus rate gives the wrong wheel angular momentum and overstates the kinetic energy.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\phi$ is the wheel angle, write $I_b\dot\theta+I_w\dot\phi=0$. Hence $\dot\theta=-(I_w/I_b)\dot\phi$ and $\Delta\theta=-(I_w/I_b)\Delta\phi$, with no need to include the wheel's carried rotation with the bus.

problems.title: Composition of two finite attitude rotations
problems.objective: Demonstrate finite-rotation noncommutativity by applying two active quarter-turns in both orders to the same basis vector.
problems.statement: Use active right-handed rotations. Compute $R=R_z(\pi/2)R_x(\pi/2)$ and its action on $\mathbf e_y$. Compute the reversed product $R'=R_x(\pi/2)R_z(\pi/2)$ on the same vector and use the results to demonstrate noncommutativity.
permittedResults: Apply the rightmost active rotation first.
problems.strategy: First: Write both active rotation matrices with one column-vector convention. Next: Multiply in the declared order and apply each product to the same test vector. Finally: Verify orthogonality and determinant one while comparing the two outputs.
hints: Write both active rotation matrices with one column-vector convention.
Multiply in the declared order and apply each product to the same test vector.
Verify orthogonality and determinant one while comparing the two outputs.
problems.solution: $R_z(\pi/2)R_x(\pi/2)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $R\mathbf e_y=\mathbf e_z$. Reversing the order gives $R'\mathbf e_y=R_x(\pi/2)(-\mathbf e_x)=-\mathbf e_x$. The distinct results prove $R_zR_x\ne R_xR_z$. Both matrices remain orthogonal with determinant one, which checks that the disagreement is order, not an invalid rotation.
rubricCriteria: Column-vector ordering produces the displayed $R_zR_x$ matrix and sends $\mathbf e_y$ to $\mathbf e_z$.
The reversed product sends the same vector to $-\mathbf e_x$, providing a direct inequivalence witness.
Orthogonality and determinant one are verified for each product without treating those properties as commutativity.

commonErrors.description: Applies the leftmost rotation first while still using column vectors.
commonErrors.consequence: Applying matrices in reading order computes a different physical sequence from the one stated.

commonErrors.description: Concludes rotations commute because both component matrices have determinant one.
commonErrors.consequence: Proper-rotation determinants certify orientation preservation, not equality of noncommuting products.

problems.flawedProof: Both products send $\mathbf e_y$ to $\mathbf e_z$ because ninety-degree rotations commute.

problems.title: Quaternion integration for constant body-axis spin
problems.objective: Integrate the unit-quaternion attitude equation for constant axial spin and connect its half-angle solution to the active rotation of a spatial vector.
problems.statement: A body starts aligned with space and rotates at constant angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$, with the same $z$ axis in body and space. Using a scalar-first unit quaternion, solve $\dot q=\tfrac12q\otimes(0,\boldsymbol\omega)$. Evaluate the attitude and the image of $\mathbf e_x$ at $t=\pi/(2\Omega)$. Check unit norm.
permittedResults: For a constant single-axis spin, exponentiate the pure-vector quaternion.
problems.strategy: First: Reduce the quaternion equation to the exponential of a constant generator. Next: Use the half-angle representation to evaluate the requested time. Finally: Rotate the test vector and verify exact unit norm.
hints: Reduce the quaternion equation to the exponential of a constant generator.
Use the half-angle representation to evaluate the requested time.
Rotate the test vector and verify exact unit norm.
problems.solution: $q(t)=(\cos(\Omega t/2),0,0,\sin(\Omega t/2))$. At $t=\pi/(2\Omega)$, $q=(\sqrt2/2,0,0,\sqrt2/2)$, representing a $90^\circ$ active rotation about $z$, so $\mathbf e_x$ maps to $\mathbf e_y$. The norm is $\cos^2(\Omega t/2)+\sin^2(\Omega t/2)=1$ for all time. Replacing the half-angle by the full angle would double the physical rotation.
rubricCriteria: The scalar-first solution uses $\cos(\Omega t/2)$ and $\sin(\Omega t/2)$ and satisfies the differential equation.
At the requested time the quaternion represents a $90^\circ$ turn carrying $\mathbf e_x$ to $\mathbf e_y$.
Unit norm is preserved for all time and the half-angle prevents a doubled physical attitude.

commonErrors.description: Uses $q=(\cos\Omega t,0,0,\sin\Omega t)$ and doubles the attitude angle.
commonErrors.consequence: Using full angles in the quaternion doubles the physical rotation and predicts the wrong image of $\mathbf e_x$.

commonErrors.description: Treats the vector part of the quaternion as the rotated spatial vector.
commonErrors.consequence: A quaternion vector part is an axis-angle parameter, not the spatial vector obtained by conjugation.

problems.flawedProof: At the requested time the quaternion is $(0,0,0,1)$, a $180^\circ$ rotation sending $\mathbf e_x$ to $-\mathbf e_x$.

problems.title: Poinsot invariant surfaces in angular-velocity space
problems.objective: Interpret torque-free Euler motion as the intersection of two invariant quadrics and prove the velocity field is tangent to each level set.
problems.statement: For a torque-free triaxial body in principal axes, show that its body angular-velocity trajectory lies on the intersection of the energy ellipsoid $\sum I_i\omega_i^2=2T$ and the angular-momentum ellipsoid $\sum I_i^2\omega_i^2=L^2$. Prove that Euler's vector field is tangent to both surfaces. Explain why their intersection is generally a curve rather than a surface.
permittedResults: Tangency follows by taking the gradients of both invariants and dotting them with $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}$.
problems.strategy: First: Identify the two exact quadratic invariants in body angular-velocity coordinates. Next: Use Euler's equations to prove both directional derivatives vanish. Finally: Count independent constraints and note the principal-axis degeneracy.
hints: Identify the two exact quadratic invariants in body angular-velocity coordinates.
Use Euler's equations to prove both directional derivatives vanish.
Count independent constraints and note the principal-axis degeneracy.
problems.solution: The two displayed equations are exactly the conserved energy and squared angular-momentum relations. Their gradients are $2(I_1\omega_1,I_2\omega_2,I_3\omega_3)$ and $2(I_1^2\omega_1,I_2^2\omega_2,I_3^2\omega_3)$. Dotting either with Euler's vector field produces the cyclic moment-difference cancellations, hence zero. The flow is therefore tangent to both level surfaces. In three-dimensional angular-velocity space, two independent scalar constraints generically intersect in a one-dimensional curve. At a principal-axis equilibrium the gradients can become dependent on the relevant component, producing a degenerate limiting intersection.
rubricCriteria: Energy and squared angular momentum are written as distinct ellipsoids in body angular-velocity coordinates.
Dot products of both gradients with Euler's vector field vanish by the correct cyclic cancellations.
Two independent constraints in three dimensions are identified as a curve, with principal-axis degeneracy treated separately.

commonErrors.description: Calls the fixed-$L$ surface a sphere in angular-velocity coordinates.
commonErrors.consequence: The fixed-angular-momentum level is generally an ellipsoid in angular-velocity space, so replacing it by a sphere distorts the polhode geometry.

commonErrors.description: Claims that conservation of two quantities freezes all three angular-velocity components.
commonErrors.consequence: Two scalar invariants leave one dynamical degree of freedom and do not freeze all three body components.

problems.flawedProof: Because $L$ is fixed, $\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2+\omega_3^2$ is fixed, so the angular-momentum level set is a sphere in angular-velocity space; its intersection with the energy ellipsoid remains a surface.

problems.title: Allowed polhode interval from two invariants
problems.objective: Use simultaneous energy and angular-momentum invariants to bound the accessible polhode interval for a concrete triaxial initial state.
problems.statement: Let $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)I_0$ and suppose a torque-free body initially has $\boldsymbol\omega=(1,1,1)\Omega_0$. Use energy and angular-momentum invariants to express $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_2^2$ in terms of $z=\omega_3^2/\Omega_0^2$. Determine the allowed interval of $z$ from nonnegativity.
permittedResults: The initial invariants are $2T=6I_0\Omega_0^2$ and $L^2=14I_0^2\Omega_0^2$.
problems.strategy: First: Evaluate both invariants at the initial condition. Next: Eliminate two squared components using the two linear equations. Finally: Impose nonnegativity and check that the initial point lies in the interval.
hints: Evaluate both invariants at the initial condition.
Eliminate two squared components using the two linear equations.
Impose nonnegativity and check that the initial point lies in the interval.
problems.solution: Set $x=\omega_1^2/\Omega_0^2$, $y=\omega_2^2/\Omega_0^2$, and $z=\omega_3^2/\Omega_0^2$. The invariants give $x+2y+3z=6$ and $x+4y+9z=14$. Subtraction yields $y+3z=4$, so $y=4-3z$, and then $x=-2+3z$. Nonnegativity requires $z\ge2/3$ and $z\le4/3$. The initial point $z=1$ lies inside the interval. These bounds are properties of the invariant intersection, not independent conservation of the body components.
rubricCriteria: The normalized invariant equations are formed with coefficients $(1,2,3)$ and their squares.
Elimination gives $y=4-3z$ and $x=-2+3z$ without assuming componentwise conservation.
Nonnegativity yields the sharp interval $2/3\le z\le4/3$ and contains the initial point.

commonErrors.description: Treats each squared body component as separately constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Treating component squares as constants eliminates the actual exchange responsible for torque-free body motion.

commonErrors.description: Forgets that the angular-momentum equation contains squared principal moments.
commonErrors.consequence: Using unsquared moments in the $L^2$ equation changes both eliminated relations and the admissible interval.

problems.flawedProof: Torque-free motion conserves each squared body component separately. Since initially $z=1$, it follows that $z=1$ for all time without combining the two global invariants.

problems.title: Angular impulse applied off a principal spin
problems.objective: Propagate a short off-axis angular impulse through a diagonal inertia tensor and quantify the externally supplied rotational energy.
problems.statement: A body is momentarily aligned with space and has principal moments $(2,3,4)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and angular velocity $(1,0,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. A short couple delivers angular impulse $(0,6,0)\,\mathrm{N\,m\,s}$ while attitude is effectively fixed. Find the post-impulse angular momentum, angular velocity, and change in rotational kinetic energy.
permittedResults: Angular impulse changes space angular momentum directly; during the short event the body and space principal axes coincide.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the pre-impulse angular momentum in the aligned principal basis. Next: Add the vector angular impulse before applying the inverse inertia tensor. Finally: Compare pre- and post-impulse energies and explain their nonconservation.
hints: Compute the pre-impulse angular momentum in the aligned principal basis.
Add the vector angular impulse before applying the inverse inertia tensor.
Compare pre- and post-impulse energies and explain their nonconservation.
problems.solution: Initially $\mathbf L^-=(2,0,0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. Thus $\mathbf L^+=(2,6,0)$ and $\boldsymbol\omega^+=\mathbf I^{-1}\mathbf L^+=(1,2,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The initial energy is $1$ J and the final energy is $\tfrac12[2(1)^2+3(2)^2]=7$ J, so $\Delta T=6$ J. Angular momentum changes by exactly the specified impulse; energy is not conserved because the applied couple does work during the impulsive rotation.
rubricCriteria: Initial and final angular momenta differ by exactly $(0,6,0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
Applying the inverse inertia tensor gives the post-impulse angular velocity $(1,2,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The energy rise from $1$ J to $7$ J is reported as actuator work rather than a conservation failure.

commonErrors.description: Adds angular impulse directly to angular velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Angular impulse changes angular momentum, not angular velocity directly; skipping inertia gives dimensionally invalid rates.

commonErrors.description: Declares kinetic energy conserved across an externally driven angular impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: An applied couple can do impulsive work, so enforcing energy conservation suppresses the actual six-joule input.

problems.flawedProof: The new angular velocity is $(1,6,0)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ because impulse and angular velocity have the same components.

problems.title: Local hyperbolic map near intermediate-axis rotation
problems.objective: Construct the signed linear hyperbolic flow near intermediate-axis rotation, including its growth eigenvector and its finite-amplitude boundary.
problems.statement: For $I_1<I_2<I_3$, linearize torque-free motion about $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_2$. Derive the $2\times2$ linear flow for perturbations $(u_1,u_3)$, its growth rate $\sigma$, and the eigenvector ratio $u_3/u_1$ for the growing branch. State why this local map does not by itself describe a complete finite-amplitude flip.
permittedResults: Keep $\omega_2=\Omega$ at zeroth order and use the first and third Euler equations.
problems.strategy: First: Linearize the correct two transverse Euler equations about the intermediate axis. Next: Multiply the off-diagonal coefficients and retain their signs to obtain the real growth rate. Finally: Find the growing eigenvector and state the domain of validity of linearization.
hints: Linearize the correct two transverse Euler equations about the intermediate axis.
Multiply the off-diagonal coefficients and retain their signs to obtain the real growth rate.
Find the growing eigenvector and state the domain of validity of linearization.
problems.solution: The linear system is $\dot u_1=[(I_2-I_3)/I_1]\Omega u_3$ and $\dot u_3=[(I_1-I_2)/I_3]\Omega u_1$. Their product is positive, giving $\ddot u_1=\sigma^2u_1$ with $\sigma=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)/(I_1I_3)}$. For the eigenvalue $+\sigma$ and positive $\Omega$, $u_3/u_1=-I_1\sigma/[(I_3-I_2)\Omega]$ under the stated signs. The map is hyperbolic and predicts exponential departure only while $|u_1|,|u_3|\ll|\Omega|$; invariants and nonlinear Euler dynamics control the subsequent flip.
rubricCriteria: The first and third Euler equations produce two signed off-diagonal coefficients whose product is positive.
The growth rate and negative growing-branch ratio follow from the same eigenvalue equation.
Linear exponential behavior is restricted to perturbations small compared with the base spin, with invariants governing later motion.

commonErrors.description: Changes both off-diagonal coefficients to positive magnitudes before finding the eigenvector sign.
commonErrors.consequence: Replacing signed coefficients by magnitudes loses the eigenvector orientation and can reverse the stability classification.

commonErrors.description: Uses exponential linear growth as an exact global solution for arbitrarily large perturbations.
commonErrors.consequence: Extrapolating a local exponential forever contradicts the bounded energy-angular-momentum intersection.

problems.flawedProof: The product of the two coefficients is negative, so intermediate-axis perturbations oscillate stably.

problems.title: Full heavy symmetric-top Lagrangian and momenta
problems.objective: Form the complete heavy symmetric-top Lagrangian in a declared Euler convention and identify exactly which canonical momenta and energy are conserved.
problems.statement: Using active $3$-$1$-$3$ Euler angles, derive the Lagrangian of a symmetric top with fixed point, moments $I_1=I_2=I$ and $I_3$, and potential $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Derive the two conserved canonical momenta and the energy. Identify the coordinate that is not cyclic.
permittedResults: Use $\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta$ and $\omega_3=\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta$.
problems.strategy: First: Express the body angular-velocity norm in the stated Euler convention. Next: Form kinetic minus potential energy and differentiate with respect to the two cyclic rates. Finally: Construct the energy and identify the noncyclic tilt coordinate.
hints: Express the body angular-velocity norm in the stated Euler convention.
Form kinetic minus potential energy and differentiate with respect to the two cyclic rates.
Construct the energy and identify the noncyclic tilt coordinate.
problems.solution: $L=\tfrac12I(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+\tfrac12I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2-Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Since $\phi$ and $\psi$ do not appear, $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$ and $p_\phi=I\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta$ are conserved. The energy is the same two positive kinetic terms plus $Mg\ell\cos\theta$. The tilt $\theta$ is not cyclic because both the kinetic metric and potential depend on it. Every term has energy dimensions.
rubricCriteria: The transverse and axial kinetic terms use the correct 3-1-3 rate combinations.
Differentiation with respect to $\dot\phi$ and $\dot\psi$ yields both conserved cyclic momenta.
The energy restores the potential with a positive sign and correctly leaves $\theta$ noncyclic.

commonErrors.description: Treats all three Euler angles as cyclic because the body is axially symmetric.
commonErrors.consequence: Axial body symmetry does not remove the tilt dependence of gravity or the Euler-angle kinetic metric.

commonErrors.description: Changes the sign of the potential between the Lagrangian and energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the potential sign between $L$ and $E$ reverses gravity while claiming to describe the same top.

problems.flawedProof: The Lagrangian is independent of $\theta$, so all three canonical momenta are conserved.

problems.title: Fast-spin stability threshold for a sleeping top
problems.objective: Determine the exact fast-spin threshold that converts the upright heavy top from exponential toppling to bounded gyroscopic oscillation.
problems.statement: A heavy symmetric top spins upright with its center of mass above the fixed point. Let its axial angular momentum be $S=I_3\omega_3$. Linearization in the two horizontal tilt components gives $I\ddot u_x+S\dot u_y-Mg\ell u_x=0$ and $I\ddot u_y-S\dot u_x-Mg\ell u_y=0$. Derive the normal-frequency equation and prove stability requires $S^2>4IMg\ell$. For $I=0.20\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $Mg\ell=0.50\,\mathrm J$, find the minimum $|S|$.
permittedResults: Use circular polarizations $u_x+iu_y\propto e^{-i\nu t}$.
problems.strategy: First: Combine the two real tilt equations into circularly polarized modes. Next: Derive the quadratic frequency condition and analyze its discriminant. Finally: Evaluate the threshold with angular-momentum units and check the zero-spin limit.
hints: Combine the two real tilt equations into circularly polarized modes.
Derive the quadratic frequency condition and analyze its discriminant.
Evaluate the threshold with angular-momentum units and check the zero-spin limit.
problems.solution: For a circular polarization the characteristic equation may be written $I\nu^2-S\nu+Mg\ell=0$ for one handedness; the other gives the sign-reversed roots. Real oscillation frequencies exist exactly when $S^2-4IMg\ell\ge0$, with strict inequality away from the marginal double root. Thus fast spin stabilizes the otherwise inverted gravitational equilibrium. Numerically $|S|_{min}=2\sqrt{IMg\ell}=2\sqrt{0.10}=0.632\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. With $S=0$, the equations reduce to exponential toppling, confirming the sign.
rubricCriteria: Circular polarization reduces the coupled tilt equations to the correct quadratic frequency equation.
The discriminant gives $S^2>4IMg\ell$ for strict linear stability and identifies the marginal double root.
The numerical threshold has angular-momentum units and the zero-spin limit recovers toppling.

commonErrors.description: Demands only $S^2>IMg\ell$ and misses the discriminant factor four.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping the factor four halves the required threshold and labels unstable slow spins as stabilized.

commonErrors.description: Calls complex frequency roots stable oscillations.
commonErrors.consequence: Complex frequencies contain exponential factors; calling them oscillations reverses the stability conclusion.

problems.flawedProof: The frequency discriminant is $S^2-IMg\ell$, so stability begins at $|S|=\sqrt{IMg\ell}=0.316\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$; the factor four is unnecessary.

problems.title: Nonintegrability of upright-disk rolling constraints
problems.objective: Prove the rolling-disk no-slip distribution is nonholonomic by testing its constraint one-forms on independent heading and spin changes.
problems.statement: An upright disk of radius $R$ has contact coordinates $(x,y)$, heading $\psi$, and spin $\phi$. With a fixed sign convention its no-slip constraints are $\dot x=R\dot\phi\cos\psi$ and $\dot y=R\dot\phi\sin\psi$. Show that these velocity constraints cannot be integrated into two configuration-only equations valid for arbitrary heading changes. Use either differential forms or a commutator of allowed motions.
permittedResults: The constraint one-forms are $dx-R\cos\psi\,d\phi$ and $dy-R\sin\psi\,d\phi$.
problems.strategy: First: Translate no slip into constraint one-forms in configuration space. Next: Differentiate the forms or compare two small allowed motion sequences with reversed order. Finally: Explain why constant heading is an integrable restriction but not the full system.
hints: Translate no slip into constraint one-forms in configuration space.
Differentiate the forms or compare two small allowed motion sequences with reversed order.
Explain why constant heading is an integrable restriction but not the full system.
problems.solution: If the first form were an exact differential constraint, its exterior derivative would vanish on every allowed displacement. Instead $d(dx-R\cos\psi\,d\phi)=R\sin\psi\,d\psi\wedge d\phi$, and the second gives $-R\cos\psi\,d\psi\wedge d\phi$. Heading and spin changes therefore generate a net transverse displacement through their commutator. The constraints are linear in velocities but nonholonomic: they restrict instantaneous motion without defining fixed surfaces in $(x,y,\psi,\phi)$ configuration space. If $\psi$ is held constant, they do integrate, which is a restricted special case rather than a contradiction.
rubricCriteria: The two velocity constraints are converted into differential one-forms on configuration space.
Their exterior derivatives remain nonzero on allowed heading-spin directions, demonstrating failed integrability.
Constant heading is separated as a restricted integrable case rather than generalized to arbitrary steering.

commonErrors.description: Integrates $x=R\phi\cos\psi$ and $y=R\phi\sin\psi$ while allowing $\psi$ to vary.
commonErrors.consequence: Integrating expressions that contain a varying heading omits product-rule terms and invents configuration equations that paths violate.

commonErrors.description: Claims every velocity-linear constraint is holonomic.
commonErrors.consequence: Linearity in velocities alone says nothing about Frobenius integrability, so it cannot establish holonomy.

problems.flawedProof: Because both equations can be integrated in time along one trajectory, they are holonomic for all trajectories.

problems.title: A sphere rolling on a rotating table
problems.objective: Solve the instantaneous no-slip constraint for a sphere whose center is fixed above a rotating table and minimize energy over the unconstrained spin.
problems.statement: A sphere of radius $R$ has center instantaneously fixed at $\mathbf r=r\mathbf e_x$ above a horizontal table rotating with $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$. Impose no slip at contact and find the required horizontal angular-velocity component of the sphere. Identify the unconstrained component. For a homogeneous sphere of mass $M$, find the minimum rotational kinetic energy compatible with no slip.
permittedResults: The table velocity is $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$ and the contact vector from the center is $-R\mathbf e_z$.
problems.strategy: First: Equate the material velocities of the two surfaces at their common point. Next: Solve the cross product for the horizontal spin and identify the null direction. Finally: Minimize over the free vertical spin and check the $r=0$ limit.
hints: Equate the material velocities of the two surfaces at their common point.
Solve the cross product for the horizontal spin and identify the null direction.
Minimize over the free vertical spin and check the $r=0$ limit.
problems.solution: No slip requires $\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\mathbf e_z)=\Omega r\mathbf e_y$. Since $\mathbf v_C=0$, this is satisfied by $\omega_x=\Omega r/R$ and $\omega_y=0$. The vertical spin $\omega_z$ is unconstrained because it produces no contact velocity. Minimum energy sets that free spin to zero. With $I=2MR^2/5$, $T_{min}=I(\Omega r/R)^2/2=M\Omega^2r^2/5$. The result vanishes at the table axis and is independent of sphere radius after substitution.
rubricCriteria: Rigid contact kinematics fixes the required horizontal angular-velocity component $\omega_x=\Omega r/R$.
Vertical spin is correctly left free because it creates no velocity at the bottom contact.
Setting that free component to zero gives $T_{min}=M\Omega^2r^2/5$ and the axis limit is consistent.

commonErrors.description: Sets the sphere angular velocity equal to the table angular velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Copying the table's vertical angular velocity onto the sphere fails to match the table's tangential contact velocity.

commonErrors.description: Treats vertical spin as fixed by no slip even though it has zero contact velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: No slip cannot determine a spin parallel to the contact radius, so assigning one removes a genuine free degree of freedom.

problems.flawedProof: No slip requires $\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$, giving energy $MR^2\Omega^2/5$.

problems.title: Intermediate-axis instability from full Euler dynamics
problems.objective: Unify Euler-equation derivation, invariant checks, all three principal-axis linearizations, and a numerical intermediate-axis e-folding time.
problems.statement: For a torque-free body with $I_1<I_2<I_3$, derive Euler's equations, prove conservation of energy and $L^2$, and linearize about each principal-axis rotation. Show the extreme axes are stable and the intermediate axis has growth rate $\sigma=|\Omega|\sqrt{(I_2-I_1)(I_3-I_2)/(I_1I_3)}$. For $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $\Omega=12.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find the e-folding time. Explain the linear-regime boundary.
permittedResults: Use the rotating-basis angular-momentum balance and retain moment-difference signs through every linearization.
problems.strategy: First: Derive the body equations from space angular-momentum balance. Next: Use two separate cyclic cancellations for the invariants, then linearize all three axes. Finally: Evaluate the intermediate growth time and state when the linear approximation ceases to apply.
hints: Derive the body equations from space angular-momentum balance.
Use two separate cyclic cancellations for the invariants, then linearize all three axes.
Evaluate the intermediate growth time and state when the linear approximation ceases to apply.
problems.solution: Euler's equations are $I_1\dot\omega_1=(I_2-I_3)\omega_2\omega_3$ and cyclic permutations. Multiplication by $\omega_i$ and by $I_i\omega_i$ gives the two cyclic cancellations proving conservation of $2T$ and $L^2$. The extreme-axis perturbations have negative second-order coefficients and oscillate. About $\Omega\mathbf e_2$, the transverse coefficient is positive, giving the stated $\sigma$. For moments $1,2,3$ and $\Omega=12$, $\sigma=12/\sqrt3=6.928\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\tau=1/\sigma=0.144\,\mathrm s$. Exponential growth applies only while transverse components remain small relative to $|\Omega|$; the exact invariants bound the subsequent nonlinear motion.
rubricCriteria: The transport theorem produces the torque-free Euler equations and both quadratic conservation laws.
Extreme-axis perturbations are oscillatory while axis 2 has the stated real growth rate.
For moments $(1,2,3)$ and $12\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the e-folding time is $0.144$ s and its linear domain is explicit.

commonErrors.description: Reverses one Euler-equation moment difference and predicts an imaginary intermediate growth rate.
commonErrors.consequence: One reversed moment difference turns a real saddle eigenvalue imaginary and falsely stabilizes the intermediate axis.

commonErrors.description: Extends the exponential perturbation solution beyond the invariant-bounded linear regime.
