commonErrors.consequence: Invariant-bounded nonlinear motion invalidates an indefinitely extrapolated linear exponential after perturbations become large.

problems.flawedProof: Reverse the sign of one linearized Euler equation. Then $\ddot u_1=-\sigma^2u_1$, so perturbations about the intermediate axis oscillate and that rotation is stable.

problems.title: Two-plane rotor balancing cancels force and rocking couple
problems.objective: Solve a two-plane dynamic-balancing problem with complex unbalance phasors and verify simultaneous cancellation of force and couple.
problems.statement: Represent each rotating unbalance by the complex phasor $U_j=m_jr_j e^{i\phi_j}$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m}$. Two existing unbalances are $U_1=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ at axial coordinate $z_1=+0.300\,\mathrm m$ and $U_2=0.0100i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ at $z_2=-0.200\,\mathrm m$. Correction masses may be placed at radius $r_c=0.100\,\mathrm m$ in planes $z_A=-0.500\,\mathrm m$ and $z_B=+0.500\,\mathrm m$. Find the two correction phasors, masses, and phases measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis so that both $\sum U$ and $\sum zU$ vanish. At $\Omega=300\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the original rotating-force and rocking-couple amplitudes and verify their corrected values.
permittedResults: A rotating unbalance produces force phasor $\Omega^2U$ and couple phasor $\Omega^2zU$ about the reference plane.
problems.strategy: First: Form the existing force and couple unbalance phasors. Next: solve the two complex linear balance equations for the correction planes. Finally: convert phasors to physical masses and phases and evaluate the before-and-after amplitudes.
hints: Static balance requires $U_A+U_B=-(U_1+U_2)$.
Dynamic balance also requires $z_AU_A+z_BU_B=-(z_1U_1+z_2U_2)$.
After solving for each complex phasor, divide its modulus by $r_c$ and use its quadrant to report the phase.
problems.solution: The original sums are $U_1+U_2=0.0200+0.0100i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ and $z_1U_1+z_2U_2=0.00600-0.00200i\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The correction equations are $U_A+U_B=-0.0200-0.0100i$ and $-0.500U_A+0.500U_B=-0.00600+0.00200i$. Solving gives $U_A=-0.00400-0.00700i$ and $U_B=-0.0160-0.00300i\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$. Thus $m_A=|U_A|/r_c=0.0806\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $240.3^\circ$ and $m_B=0.1628\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $190.6^\circ$. Before correction the force amplitude is $\Omega^2|\sum U|=2.01\times10^3\,\mathrm N$ and the couple amplitude is $\Omega^2|\sum zU|=5.69\times10^2\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Substitution gives both corrected phasor sums exactly zero, so both amplitudes vanish for every $\Omega$ within the rigid-rotor model.
rubricCriteria: Both complex balance equations are formed with the correct axial signs and solved as $U_A=-0.00400-0.00700i$ and $U_B=-0.0160-0.00300i$.
Phasor moduli and quadrants give masses $0.0806$ kg and $0.1628$ kg at $240.3^\circ$ and $190.6^\circ$.
Original force and couple amplitudes evaluate to $2.01$ kN and $569$ N m, and direct substitution verifies both corrected sums vanish.

commonErrors.description: Balances only $\sum U$ with one correction and ignores the axial couple $\sum zU$.
commonErrors.consequence: Static balance can remove the net rotating force while leaving a nonzero rocking couple.

commonErrors.description: Uses phasor components as unsigned mass values and discards their phases.
commonErrors.consequence: Correction masses placed without the computed quadrants reinforce rather than cancel some unbalance components.

problems.flawedProof: Choose one correction $U_A=-(U_1+U_2)$, so $\sum U=0$. The rotor is therefore fully balanced; axial locations and the separate sum $\sum zU$ are irrelevant.

problems.title: Planar gravity-gradient libration of a dumbbell satellite
problems.objective: Extract the exact gravity-gradient attitude equation and compare its small-libration period with the orbital period.
problems.statement: A slender dumbbell satellite is in a circular orbit of mean motion $n$. Let $\theta$ be its small in-plane angle from the local radial direction. Starting from the quadrupole gravity-gradient potential $U(\theta)=-(3/2)n^2(I_t-I_r)\cos^2\theta$ and rotational kinetic energy $I_n\dot\theta^2/2$, derive the exact angular equation and its small-libration frequency when the planar inertia relation gives $(I_t-I_r)/I_n=1$. Compare the libration period with the orbital period.
permittedResults: Differentiate the supplied attitude potential before linearizing.
problems.strategy: First: Form the attitude equation from the supplied potential and rotational inertia. Next: Linearize only after obtaining the exact sine-cosine torque. Finally: Compare periods and check the equilibrium curvature sign.
hints: Form the attitude equation from the supplied potential and rotational inertia.
Linearize only after obtaining the exact sine-cosine torque.
Compare periods and check the equilibrium curvature sign.
problems.solution: $I_n\ddot\theta=-dU/d\theta=-3n^2(I_t-I_r)\sin\theta\cos\theta$. With the stated inertia ratio, $\ddot\theta+3n^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$. For small angle, $\sin\theta\cos\theta\simeq\theta$, so $\omega_{lib}=\sqrt3n$. Therefore $T_{lib}=2\pi/(\sqrt3n)=T_{orbit}/\sqrt3$. The radial alignment is stable because $U''(0)=3n^2(I_t-I_r)>0$ under the stated ordering; the tangential alignment has the opposite curvature.
rubricCriteria: Differentiation of the cosine-squared potential includes the factor two and the correct restoring sign.
The stated inertia ratio reduces the linear frequency to $\sqrt3n$.
Curvature classifies radial alignment as stable and gives $T_{lib}=T_{orbit}/\sqrt3$.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $\cos^2\theta$ without the factor two.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing the derivative factor two lowers the torque and frequency by a spurious factor of $\sqrt2$.

commonErrors.description: Uses orbital mean motion $n$ itself as the libration frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Orbital rotation supplies the scale $n$ but the gravity-gradient curvature changes the libration frequency.

problems.flawedProof: Differentiate $\cos^2\theta$ as $-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, missing its factor two. This gives $\omega_{lib}=\sqrt{3/2}n$ and $T_{lib}=\sqrt{2/3}T_{orbit}$.

problems.title: Oblique spinning-rod impact through effective mass
problems.objective: Reduce an oblique spinning-rod collision to a scalar contact effective mass and verify restitution after coupled translation and rotation.
problems.statement: A uniform slender rod of mass $M$ and length $2a$ lies in a vertical plane at angle $\gamma$ above horizontal. Its lower-left endpoint, with center-to-contact vector $\mathbf r=(-a\cos\gamma,-a\sin\gamma)$, strikes a fixed smooth horizontal plane. Before impact the center vertical velocity is $V_y^-$ and the counterclockwise spin is $\omega^-$. Derive the contact normal speed, effective inverse mass, normal impulse for restitution coefficient $e$, and post-impact $(V_y^+,\omega^+)$. Show angular momentum about contact is conserved during impact. Evaluate for $M=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $a=0.750\,\mathrm m$, $\gamma=30.0^\circ$, $V_y^-=-2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\omega^-=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $e=0.500$, using $I_C=Ma^2/3$.
permittedResults: With upward normal and $r_x=-a\cos\gamma$, the signed contact speed is $g^-=V_y^-+\omega^-r_x<0$.
problems.strategy: First: Write the pre-impact contact velocity from rigid-body kinematics in the declared axes. Next: Propagate one normal impulse through both center translation and angular impulse to obtain the contact effective mass. Finally: Apply restitution, recompute the contact speed numerically, and verify angular momentum about contact.
hints: Write the pre-impact contact velocity from rigid-body kinematics in the declared axes.
Propagate one normal impulse through both center translation and angular impulse to obtain the contact effective mass.
Apply restitution, recompute the contact speed numerically, and verify angular momentum about contact.
problems.solution: An upward impulse $J$ gives $V_y^+=V_y^-+J/M$ and $\omega^+=\omega^-+r_xJ/I_C$. Hence $g^+=g^-+J\mathcal K$ with $\mathcal K=1/M+r_x^2/I_C>0$. Restitution $g^+=-eg^-$ gives $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K$. Because the plane impulse acts at contact, its moment about contact vanishes; with gravity negligible, angular momentum about that point is unchanged. Numerically $I_C=0.750\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $r_x=-0.6495\,\mathrm m$, $g^-=-2.6495\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\mathcal K=0.8125\,\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$. Thus $J=4.891\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, $V_y^+=-0.777\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\omega^+=-3.236\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The reconstructed $g^+=1.3248\,\mathrm{m/s}=-eg^-$ checks every sign.
rubricCriteria: Rigid-body kinematics gives $g^-=V_y^-+\omega^-r_x$ at the actual endpoint.
Impulse updates produce $\mathcal K=1/M+r_x^2/I_C$ and $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K$.
The numerical post-impact state reconstructs $g^+=-eg^-$ and preserves angular momentum about contact.

commonErrors.description: Applies restitution to the center velocity instead of the velocity of the oblique spinning contact point.
commonErrors.consequence: Applying restitution at the center ignores pre-impact spin and predicts the wrong normal impulse.

commonErrors.description: Drops the rotational term $r_x^2/I_C$ from the effective inverse mass.
commonErrors.consequence: Omitting rotational compliance overestimates the impulse because all contact-speed change is assigned to translation.

problems.flawedProof: A smooth plane cannot change rod spin, so the center alone rebounds with speed $-eV_y^-$.

problems.title: Euler-top quadrature from invariant elimination
problems.objective: Eliminate two squared Euler-top components from the invariant pair and reduce the remaining motion to an explicit cubic quadrature.
problems.statement: Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$, $A=2T$, $B=L^2$, and $y=\omega_2^2$. Eliminate $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_3^2$ from the two invariants, then derive a first-order cubic equation $(\dot y)^2=P_3(y)$. State the quadrature for one oscillation between adjacent nonnegative turning roots. No special-function name may replace the derivation.
permittedResults: Use Euler's second equation only after solving the two linear invariant equations.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the pair of invariant equations linearly for the other two squared components. Next: Square the second Euler equation only after multiplying by $2\omega_2$. Finally: Identify allowed roots, write the round-trip quadrature, and check dimensions.
hints: Solve the pair of invariant equations linearly for the other two squared components.
Square the second Euler equation only after multiplying by $2\omega_2$.
Identify allowed roots, write the round-trip quadrature, and check dimensions.
problems.solution: Invariant elimination gives $\omega_1^2=[I_3A-B-I_2(I_3-I_2)y]/[I_1(I_3-I_1)]$ and $\omega_3^2=[B-I_1A-I_2(I_2-I_1)y]/[I_3(I_3-I_1)]$. Since $\dot y=2\omega_2\dot\omega_2=2[(I_3-I_1)/I_2]\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3$, squaring yields $P_3(y)=4y[I_3A-B-I_2(I_3-I_2)y][B-I_1A-I_2(I_2-I_1)y]/(I_1I_2^2I_3)$. If $y_-$ and $y_+$ are adjacent allowed roots, the oscillation period is $2\int_{y_-}^{y_+}dy/\sqrt{P_3(y)}$. Dimensional inspection gives $(\dot y)^2$ units $\mathrm{s^{-6}}$ on both sides.
rubricCriteria: Linear algebra is applied to $\omega_1^2$ and $\omega_3^2$ with the denominators and moment order intact.
Differentiating $y=\omega_2^2$ supplies $2\omega_2$ before Euler's second equation is squared.
The cubic, its allowed adjacent roots, round-trip period integral, and $\mathrm{s^{-6}}$ dimensions are all consistent.

commonErrors.description: Eliminates unsquared angular-velocity components linearly from quadratic invariants.
commonErrors.consequence: Quadratic invariants do not support linear elimination of signed angular velocities, so that route creates false branches.

commonErrors.description: Forgets the factor $2\omega_2$ when differentiating $y=\omega_2^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Losing $2\omega_2$ changes the polynomial degree and the temporal dimensions of the reduced equation.

problems.flawedProof: Solve the two quadratic invariants linearly for the unsquared variables $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$. Substitution makes $\dot y$ linear in $y$, so no cubic polynomial is needed.

problems.title: Dzhanibekov flip time on the Euler separatrix
problems.objective: Construct the Euler-separatrix model of a Dzhanibekov flip and quantify its logarithmically diverging near-endpoint flip time.
problems.statement: To model a Dzhanibekov, or tennis-racket, flip for $I_1<I_2<I_3$, consider the torque-free separatrix with $2T=L^2/I_2$ and define $\Omega=L/I_2>0$. Verify a heteroclinic solution with $\omega_2=\Omega\tanh(\sigma t)$ and transverse components proportional to $\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$. Derive $\sigma$, the two transverse amplitudes, and the time to go from $\omega_2=-\Omega(1-\delta)$ to $+\Omega(1-\delta)$. Evaluate it for $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\Omega=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\delta=0.0100$.
permittedResults: Use both invariants to determine transverse amplitudes before applying Euler's second equation.
problems.strategy: First: Use the separatrix energy relation in both quadratic invariants. Next: Match the hyperbolic-function ansatz to Euler's equations to determine amplitudes and growth scale. Finally: Solve the two threshold times, evaluate them, and identify the logarithmic divergence.
hints: Use the separatrix energy relation in both quadratic invariants.
Match the hyperbolic-function ansatz to Euler's equations to determine amplitudes and growth scale.
Solve the two threshold times, evaluate them, and identify the logarithmic divergence.
problems.solution: The invariant relations give $\omega_1=\Omega\sqrt{I_2(I_3-I_2)/[I_1(I_3-I_1)]}\,\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$ and $\omega_3=\Omega\sqrt{I_2(I_2-I_1)/[I_3(I_3-I_1)]}\,\operatorname{sech}(\sigma t)$, up to consistent signs. Euler's second equation then gives $\sigma=\Omega\sqrt{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)/(I_1I_3)}$. The requested interval is $\Delta t=2\operatorname{artanh}(1-\delta)/\sigma=\ln[(2-\delta)/\delta]/\sigma$. Numerically $\sigma=10/\sqrt3=5.7735\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\Delta t=\ln199/5.7735=0.917\,\mathrm s$. As $\delta\to0$, the time diverges logarithmically; the exact separatrix is not periodic.
rubricCriteria: Both invariants fix the transverse $\operatorname{sech}$ amplitudes with the correct moment ratios.
Euler's equation supplies $\sigma=\Omega\sqrt{(I_3-I_2)(I_2-I_1)/(I_1I_3)}$.
The threshold-to-threshold time reduces to $\ln[(2-\delta)/\delta]/\sigma$ and evaluates to $0.917$ s.

commonErrors.description: Calls the exact heteroclinic separatrix a finite-period orbit.
commonErrors.consequence: A heteroclinic orbit approaches equilibria asymptotically, so assigning it a finite period erases the logarithmic delay.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\sigma=\Omega$ independent of all principal moments.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring principal moments gives the wrong local growth scale and therefore the wrong flip-time estimate.

problems.flawedProof: The flip period is $2\pi/\Omega=0.628\,\mathrm s$ because the body rotates once about the intermediate axis.

problems.title: Heavy-top nutation separatrix and double-root test
problems.objective: Characterize a heavy-top nutation separatrix as an unstable double turning root and prove its logarithmic approach time locally.
problems.statement: For the heavy symmetric-top effective potential $U_{eff}(\theta)=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$, prove that a nutation separatrix occurs when the energy line has a double root at an unstable stationary angle $\theta_s$. Derive the two algebraic conditions and show the travel time to $\theta_s$ diverges logarithmically when $U_{eff}''(\theta_s)<0$.
permittedResults: Near the stationary angle, expand $E-U_{eff}$ through quadratic order.
problems.strategy: First: State both energy equality and vanishing derivative at the proposed separatrix angle. Next: Expand the effective potential locally and insert it into the nutation energy equation. Finally: Compare the logarithmic double-root time with an ordinary simple turning point.
hints: State both energy equality and vanishing derivative at the proposed separatrix angle.
Expand the effective potential locally and insert it into the nutation energy equation.
Compare the logarithmic double-root time with an ordinary simple turning point.
problems.solution: A double turning root requires $E_s=U_{eff}(\theta_s)$ and $U_{eff}'(\theta_s)=0$. If the stationary point is unstable, $U_{eff}''(\theta_s)<0$. Writing $q=\theta-\theta_s$ gives $E_s-U_{eff}(\theta)=-(1/2)U_{eff}''(\theta_s)q^2+O(q^3)$. From $I\dot\theta^2/2=E_s-U_{eff}$, $dt\sim\sqrt{I/[-U_{eff}''(\theta_s)]}\,dq/|q|$. Its integral diverges as $\ln|q|^{-1}$. A simple turning root would instead give an integrable inverse-square-root singularity, so stationarity is essential.
rubricCriteria: Both $E_s=U_{eff}(\theta_s)$ and $U_{eff}'(\theta_s)=0$ are imposed at the candidate root.
Negative curvature turns the local energy difference into a positive quadratic in displacement.
The resulting $dq/|q|$ time integral is contrasted with the integrable square-root behavior of a simple turning point.

commonErrors.description: Identifies every ordinary turning point as a separatrix.
commonErrors.consequence: An ordinary simple root produces a finite reflection time and therefore is not automatically a separatrix.

commonErrors.description: Uses a stable minimum with positive curvature to claim logarithmic approach.
commonErrors.consequence: Expansion about a stable minimum has the wrong curvature sign for asymptotic approach at the same energy.

problems.flawedProof: Only $E=U_{eff}(\theta_s)$ is needed; the derivative can be nonzero and the time still diverges logarithmically.

problems.title: Routh reduction of the heavy symmetric top
problems.objective: Perform a genuine partial Legendre transform of the heavy top at fixed axial momentum and verify the reduced dynamics.
problems.statement: For the heavy symmetric-top Lagrangian in problem CM:185, hold $p_\psi$ fixed and eliminate the cyclic rate $\dot\psi$. Derive the Routhian $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$ as a function of $(\theta,\phi,\dot\theta,\dot\phi;p_\psi)$. Verify that its $\phi$ momentum is still $p_\phi$ and that its reduced Euler-Lagrange equation for $\theta$ matches the full equation after elimination.
permittedResults: Solve $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$ before performing the partial Legendre transform.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the cyclic momentum relation exactly. Next: Perform the partial Legendre transform rather than mere substitution into the Lagrangian. Finally: Check the surviving cyclic momentum and compare the reduced tilt equation term by term.
hints: Solve the cyclic momentum relation exactly.
Perform the partial Legendre transform rather than mere substitution into the Lagrangian.
Check the surviving cyclic momentum and compare the reduced tilt equation term by term.
problems.solution: The eliminated rate is $\dot\psi=p_\psi/I_3-\dot\phi\cos\theta$. Substitution into $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$ gives $\mathcal R=\tfrac12I(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta-p_\psi^2/(2I_3)-Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Its momentum is $\partial\mathcal R/\partial\dot\phi=I\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta=p_\phi$. Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ produces the same centrifugal, gyroscopic, and gravitational terms as the full $\theta$ equation with the eliminated rate. The negative constant $-p_\psi^2/(2I_3)$ does not affect reduced trajectories.
rubricCriteria: The axial rate is solved from $p_\psi$ before forming $\mathcal R=L-p_\psi\dot\psi$.
The Routhian retains the gyroscopic $p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta$ term and has the correct negative axial constant.
Its surviving $\phi$ momentum and $\theta$ equation agree with the full eliminated system.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the eliminated rate into $L$ but omits the $-p_\psi\dot\psi$ term.
commonErrors.consequence: Substitution into $L$ alone is not Routh reduction and leaves the cyclic sector with the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Drops the gyroscopic term $p_\psi\dot\phi\cos\theta$ as a total derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The gyroscopic term depends on $\theta$ and affects reduced motion; discarding it is not a harmless boundary change.

problems.flawedProof: The reduced Lagrangian is obtained by deleting every term containing $\psi$ or $p_\psi$.

problems.title: Two-impulse rest-to-rest attitude maneuver
problems.objective: Optimize a bounded-torque rest-to-rest principal-axis maneuver and compute its switching data and impulse budget.
problems.statement: A spacecraft rotates about one principal axis with moment $I$. It starts and ends at rest and must rotate through angle $\Theta>0$. An actuator can apply torques $+\tau$ and $-\tau$ of fixed magnitude, switching once. Derive the minimum-time symmetric maneuver, switch time, peak angular speed, total time, and angular impulse magnitude of each burn. Evaluate for $I=120\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\tau=24.0\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, and $\Theta=\pi/2$.
permittedResults: With bounded torque and no speed limit, accelerate at full torque then decelerate at full opposite torque.
problems.strategy: First: Use the torque bound to identify full positive and negative acceleration arcs. Next: Integrate angular speed and angle on both symmetric phases. Finally: Evaluate the switch quantities and verify zero final angular momentum.
hints: Use the torque bound to identify full positive and negative acceleration arcs.
Integrate angular speed and angle on both symmetric phases.
Evaluate the switch quantities and verify zero final angular momentum.
problems.solution: The angular acceleration magnitude is $a=\tau/I$. Symmetry gives half the angle during each phase: $\Theta=at_s^2$, so $t_s=\sqrt{I\Theta/\tau}$. The peak speed is $at_s=\sqrt{\tau\Theta/I}$ and total time is $2t_s$. Each burn has angular impulse $\tau t_s=\sqrt{I\tau\Theta}$. Numerically $a=0.200\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $t_s=\sqrt{7.85398}=2.802\,\mathrm s$, $\omega_{max}=0.560\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, total time $5.605$ s, and each impulse $67.3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. Opposite impulses give zero final angular momentum.
rubricCriteria: Time symmetry splits the rotation into equal acceleration and deceleration phases.
The relation $\Theta=at_s^2$ yields the switch time, peak speed, and total time with correct factors.
The numerical impulses are equal and opposite, returning angular momentum to zero after a $\pi/2$ turn.

commonErrors.description: Accelerates for the whole maneuver and assumes the spacecraft can stop without a second impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: A single positive burn cannot satisfy the final-rest boundary condition, regardless of its displacement time.

commonErrors.description: Sets each half-phase displacement equal to $at_s^2$ instead of $at_s^2/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Doubling each half-phase displacement underestimates the switch time and leaves the integrated angle inconsistent.

problems.flawedProof: The minimum time is $\sqrt{2I\Theta/\tau}$ with only one positive torque burn.

problems.title: Small-angle stability of a rolling convex body
problems.objective: Relate local contact curvature to the quadratic rocking stability and frequency of a rolling convex body.
problems.statement: A smooth convex body rocks without slip in a vertical plane about an equilibrium contact. Its center of mass is height $h$ above contact, the local radius of curvature of the boundary is $\rho$, and the central moment about the out-of-plane axis is $I_C$. Show that to quadratic order the center height changes by $(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ and the kinetic energy is $(I_C+Mh^2)\dot\theta^2/2$. Derive the stability condition and small-rocking frequency. Apply it to an elliptical cross-section with horizontal semi-axis $a$ and vertical semi-axis $b$, for which $\rho=a^2/b$ at the bottom.
permittedResults: Use rolling geometry only to second order around the equilibrium contact.
problems.strategy: First: Expand both rolling geometry and kinetic energy consistently to quadratic order. Next: Build the small-angle Lagrangian and read the curvature sign and frequency. Finally: Insert the ellipse curvature and check broad, tall, and circular limits.
hints: Expand both rolling geometry and kinetic energy consistently to quadratic order.
Build the small-angle Lagrangian and read the curvature sign and frequency.
Insert the ellipse curvature and check broad, tall, and circular limits.
problems.solution: The quadratic Lagrangian is $L=(I_C+Mh^2)\dot\theta^2/2-Mg(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ up to constants. Hence $(I_C+Mh^2)\ddot\theta+Mg(\rho-h)\theta=0$. Stability requires $\rho>h$, with frequency $\omega=\sqrt{Mg(\rho-h)/(I_C+Mh^2)}$; equality is neutral at this order and $\rho<h$ is unstable. For the ellipse with its center at height $h=b$, $\rho-h=(a^2-b^2)/b$, so the broad orientation $a>b$ is stable and the tall orientation $a<b$ is unstable. A circle $a=b$ is neutrally indifferent, a useful limit check.
rubricCriteria: Geometry gives center-height change $(\rho-h)\theta^2/2$ under the declared displacement.
The effective inertia includes both $I_C$ and the center translation term $Mh^2$.
The sign of $\rho-h$ classifies ellipse orientations and the circular limit becomes neutral.

commonErrors.description: Uses $h-\rho$ instead of $\rho-h$ and reverses broad-versus-tall stability.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing the height-curvature difference swaps stable broad bodies with unstable tall ones.

commonErrors.description: Omits the translational contribution $Mh^2$ from the effective inertia.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping $Mh^2$ makes the predicted frequency too high by ignoring center-of-mass kinetic energy.

problems.flawedProof: The height change is $(h-\rho)\theta^2/2$, so broad ellipses with $a>b$ have negative curvature energy and are unstable, while tall ellipses are stable.

problems.title: General frictionless rigid-body collision impulse
problems.objective: Derive the normal impulse between two offset rigid bodies from their full translational and rotational contact compliance.
problems.statement: Two free rigid bodies contact at points with center-to-contact vectors $\mathbf r_A$ and $\mathbf r_B$. Let the unit normal $\mathbf n$ point from $B$ to $A$, and let the pre-impact relative normal speed $g^-=(\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega_A\times\mathbf r_A-\mathbf v_B-\boldsymbol\omega_B\times\mathbf r_B)\cdot\mathbf n<0$. Derive the frictionless impulse magnitude $J$ for coefficient of restitution $e$, including both rotational effective-mass terms. State the positivity condition on the denominator.
permittedResults: Apply impulses $+J\mathbf n$ to $A$ and $-J\mathbf n$ to $B$, then update both spins by angular impulse.
problems.strategy: First: Write linear and angular impulse updates for both bodies with one normal convention. Next: Project the resulting contact-point relative velocity onto the normal. Finally: Apply restitution, prove denominator positivity, and check the central-impact limit.
hints: Write linear and angular impulse updates for both bodies with one normal convention.
Project the resulting contact-point relative velocity onto the normal.
Apply restitution, prove denominator positivity, and check the central-impact limit.
problems.solution: The velocity updates are $\Delta\mathbf v_A=J\mathbf n/m_A$, $\Delta\boldsymbol\omega_A=\mathbf I_A^{-1}(\mathbf r_A\times J\mathbf n)$, with opposite linear and corresponding angular impulses for $B$. The relative normal change is $J\mathcal K$, where $\mathcal K=1/m_A+1/m_B+(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_A^{-1}(\mathbf r_A\times\mathbf n)+(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)\cdot\mathbf I_B^{-1}(\mathbf r_B\times\mathbf n)$. Restitution $g^+=-eg^-$ gives $J=-(1+e)g^-/\mathcal K>0$. For positive masses and positive-definite inertia on the relevant rotational subspaces, $\mathcal K>0$. If both contact arms are parallel to $\mathbf n$, the rotational terms vanish and the particle formula returns.
rubricCriteria: Opposite impulses update both center velocities and both angular velocities with consistent contact arms.
The effective inverse mass contains two positive translational terms and both inertia-weighted rotational terms.
Restitution gives a positive impulse for closing contact and recovers the particle limit when both arms are normal.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the reduced translational mass and omits both rotational contact responses.
commonErrors.consequence: Using only reduced translational mass ignores contact-point motion generated by angular impulse.

commonErrors.description: Applies impulses in the same direction to both bodies.
commonErrors.consequence: Impulses in the same direction violate action-reaction and create spurious net momentum in the isolated pair.

problems.flawedProof: The impulse is $-(1+e)g^-/(1/m_A+1/m_B)$ for every rigid-body contact, regardless of contact offset.

problems.title: Offset-thruster translation and rotation audit
problems.objective: Separate translation and rotation from an offset spacecraft thruster and reconcile the acquired kinetic energy with constant-force work.
problems.statement: A free spacecraft has mass $M=500\,\mathrm{kg}$ and principal inertia $\operatorname{diag}(800,1000,1200)\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. It is initially at rest and aligned with space. A constant body force $\mathbf F=(0,200,0)\,\mathrm N$ acts for $4.00$ s at body point $\mathbf r=(2.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$. Neglect attitude change during the burn. Find the linear and angular impulses, post-burn center velocity, angular velocity, and kinetic energy. Reconcile the energy with the impulse process rather than assuming impulse times final velocity.
permittedResults: Use $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ and integrate both impulse balances in the frozen attitude.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate the force and its moment about the center over the fixed-attitude burn. Next: Apply inverse mass and inverse inertia to the two impulses. Finally: Compute both kinetic-energy parts and check the constant-acceleration work factor.
hints: Integrate the force and its moment about the center over the fixed-attitude burn.
Apply inverse mass and inverse inertia to the two impulses.
Compute both kinetic-energy parts and check the constant-acceleration work factor.
problems.solution: The linear impulse is $(0,800,0)\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, so $\mathbf v_C=(0,1.60,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The torque is $(0,0,400)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ and angular impulse is $(0,0,1600)\,\mathrm{N\,m\,s}$, giving $\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,1600/1200)=(0,0,4/3)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Translational energy is $640$ J and rotational energy is $\tfrac12(1200)(16/9)=1066.7$ J, totaling $1706.7$ J. For constant forces accelerating from rest, work equals one half of impulse dotted with final generalized velocity, not impulse times final velocity; the latter would double both contributions.
rubricCriteria: Linear impulse produces $1.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$ center velocity while the offset torque produces $4/3\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ spin.
Translational and rotational energies evaluate to $640$ J and $1066.7$ J.
Half of generalized impulse dotted with final generalized velocity explains the $1706.7$ J total from rest.

commonErrors.description: Uses the force application point as the translational reference and omits center-of-mass motion.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the application point as the translating reference loses center-of-mass dynamics and misallocates the impulse.

commonErrors.description: Computes work as impulse dotted with final velocity, doubling the energy acquired from rest.
commonErrors.consequence: Impulse dotted with final velocity is twice the work for constant acceleration from rest, so it doubles both energy channels.

problems.flawedProof: The offset does not matter in free space, so the spacecraft only translates and acquires $1280$ J.

problems.title: Regular Legendre transform of a natural Lagrangian
problems.objective: Convert a regular natural Lagrangian into canonical variables and verify that Hamilton and Euler-Lagrange evolution agree.
problems.statement: For $L(q,\dot q)=m\dot q^2/2-V(q)$ with $m>0$, compute the canonical momentum, invert the velocity-momentum relation, and construct the Hamiltonian. Verify Hamilton's equations reproduce the Euler-Lagrange equation and identify the regularity condition.
permittedResults: Use $H=p\dot q-L$ only after expressing $\dot q$ in terms of $(q,p)$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to velocity and check the Hessian. Next: Invert for velocity before evaluating the Legendre transform. Finally: Apply both Hamilton equations and recover the second-order equation.
hints: Differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to velocity and check the Hessian.
Invert for velocity before evaluating the Legendre transform.
Apply both Hamilton equations and recover the second-order equation.
problems.solution: The momentum is $p=\partial L/\partial\dot q=m\dot q$, so $\dot q=p/m$. The Legendre transform is $H=p(p/m)-[p^2/(2m)-V]=p^2/(2m)+V(q)$. Hamilton's equations give $\dot q=p/m$ and $\dot p=-V'(q)$, hence $m\ddot q+V'(q)=0$, exactly Euler-Lagrange. The velocity Hessian is $\partial^2L/\partial\dot q^2=m$, which is nonzero because $m>0$; this is the required regularity. Kinetic and potential terms both have energy dimensions.
rubricCriteria: The velocity Hessian $m$ is identified as invertible and gives $p=m\dot q$.
Eliminating velocity from the Legendre transform produces $H=p^2/(2m)+V(q)$.
Hamilton's two first-order equations recombine to $m\ddot q+V'(q)=0$ with energy dimensions intact.

commonErrors.description: Leaves $\dot q$ inside the alleged Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: A Hamiltonian containing unresolved velocity is not a function on canonical phase space and cannot generate the requested equations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $H=L-p\dot q$ and reverses both energy terms.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing the Legendre transform changes kinetic and potential signs and yields dynamics opposite to the Lagrangian system.

problems.flawedProof: Since $p=m\dot q$, the Hamiltonian is $p^2/m-V(q)$ and gives the same equation.

problems.title: Hamiltonian solution of the harmonic oscillator
problems.objective: Solve oscillator Hamilton equations as an exact symplectic phase-space map and verify both its invariant quadratic energy and unit determinant.
problems.statement: For $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, solve Hamilton's equations with $q(0)=q_0$ and $p(0)=p_0$. Express the phase-space map as a matrix and verify it preserves both energy and determinant one.
permittedResults: Differentiate once more to obtain $\ddot q+\omega^2q=0$.
problems.strategy: First: Write both first-order Hamilton equations. Next: Solve the resulting oscillator while preserving both initial data. Finally: Check determinant, energy, and the zero-time identity.
hints: Write both first-order Hamilton equations.
Solve the resulting oscillator while preserving both initial data.
Check determinant, energy, and the zero-time identity.
problems.solution: Hamilton's equations are $\dot q=p/m$ and $\dot p=-m\omega^2q$. Thus $q(t)=q_0\cos\omega t+[p_0/(m\omega)]\sin\omega t$ and $p(t)=p_0\cos\omega t-m\omega q_0\sin\omega t$. The map matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t/(m\omega)\\-m\omega\sin\omega t&\cos\omega t\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is one, and direct substitution cancels cross terms in $p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, proving exact energy preservation. At $t=0$ it is the identity.
rubricCriteria: Initial data propagate through the correct sine-cosine formulas with reciprocal $m\omega$ scalings.
The matrix determinant is one and its $t=0$ value is the identity.
Substitution into the Hamiltonian cancels cross terms and proves exact energy preservation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p=mq$ instead of $p=m\dot q$.
commonErrors.consequence: Confusing coordinate with velocity removes the canonical momentum scale and makes the phase map dimensionally inconsistent.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the same sign in both off-diagonal matrix entries.
commonErrors.consequence: Equal off-diagonal signs produce a hyperbolic matrix rather than bounded oscillator rotation.

problems.flawedProof: Set $p=mq$ instead of $p=m\dot q$. Then both phase coordinates have the same scale and the flow is the Euclidean rotation $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t\\-\sin\omega t&\cos\omega t\end{pmatrix}$, independent of $m$.

problems.title: Energy ellipse and enclosed action of an oscillator
problems.objective: Compute the oscillator's phase ellipse, enclosed symplectic area, and normalized action directly from a fixed energy.
problems.statement: For the oscillator Hamiltonian $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, characterize the constant-energy curve $H=E>0$, find its intercepts, calculate its enclosed phase-space area, and evaluate the action $J=(2\pi)^{-1}\oint p\,dq$.
permittedResults: Use the geometric area of an ellipse after finding its $q$ and $p$ semiaxes.
problems.strategy: First: Find the two semiaxes by setting one phase coordinate to zero. Next: Multiply them to obtain the phase-space ellipse area. Finally: Normalize by $2\pi$ and check action dimensions and the zero-energy limit.
hints: Find the two semiaxes by setting one phase coordinate to zero.
Multiply them to obtain the phase-space ellipse area.
Normalize by $2\pi$ and check action dimensions and the zero-energy limit.
problems.solution: The intercepts are $q_{max}=\sqrt{2E/(m\omega^2)}$ and $p_{max}=\sqrt{2mE}$. The phase curve is an ellipse. Its area is $\pi q_{max}p_{max}=2\pi E/\omega$, so $J=E/\omega$. The result has action units because energy divided by angular frequency is $\mathrm{J\,s}$. As $E\to0$, both intercepts and the area vanish.
rubricCriteria: Coordinate and momentum intercepts are found with their different mass-frequency scalings.
Their product gives area $2\pi E/\omega$ rather than a configuration-space square.
Division by $2\pi$ yields $J=E/\omega$ with action units and the zero-energy limit.

commonErrors.description: Uses the configuration-space amplitude twice when computing phase area.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the coordinate amplitude for both axes ignores momentum units and creates a dimensionally impossible area.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor $2\pi$ in the action definition.
commonErrors.consequence: Without the $2\pi$ normalization, the reported quantity is enclosed phase area rather than the defined action.

problems.flawedProof: The area is $\pi E^2$ because both axes are proportional to energy.

problems.title: A nontrivial Poisson-bracket calculation
problems.objective: Evaluate a polynomial Poisson bracket by derivatives and independently check its coefficient through algebraic bracket rules.
problems.statement: In one canonical pair define $f(q,p)=q^2p$ and $g(q,p)=qp^2$. Compute $\{f,g\}$ directly. Independently reproduce it using antisymmetry and the Leibniz rule. State the dimensions if $q$ is length and $p$ is momentum.
permittedResults: Use $\{f,g\}=f_qg_p-f_pg_q$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate each polynomial with respect to both canonical variables. Next: Subtract the cross products in the declared bracket order. Finally: Check the result with Leibniz expansion, antisymmetry, and dimensions.
hints: Differentiate each polynomial with respect to both canonical variables.
Subtract the cross products in the declared bracket order.
Check the result with Leibniz expansion, antisymmetry, and dimensions.
problems.solution: The derivatives are $f_q=2qp$, $f_p=q^2$, $g_q=p^2$, and $g_p=2qp$. Therefore $\{f,g\}=4q^2p^2-q^2p^2=3q^2p^2$. Expanding products with $\{q,p\}=1$ gives the same coefficient. The bracket has dimensions $q^2p^2$, equal to the product dimensions of $f$ and $g$ divided by one action, as the derivative definition requires. Reversing the arguments gives $-3q^2p^2$.
rubricCriteria: All four partial derivatives are computed before forming the ordered cross products.
Subtraction gives $3q^2p^2$ and antisymmetry gives the negative reversed bracket.
Leibniz expansion and action-based dimensional analysis agree with the direct result.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two cross products instead of subtracting them.
commonErrors.consequence: Adding the cross products changes the coefficient from three to five and violates the bracket definition.

commonErrors.description: Treats $q$ and $p$ as commuting under the Poisson bracket and returns zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Ordinary commutativity of products does not make canonical Poisson brackets vanish.

problems.flawedProof: Add rather than subtract the derivative cross products: $\{f,g\}=4q^2p^2+q^2p^2=5q^2p^2$.

problems.title: An explicitly time-dependent oscillator invariant
problems.objective: Test an explicitly time-dependent oscillator candidate honestly, replace the false claim with two true quadrature invariants, and reconstruct the trajectory.
problems.statement: For $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, audit the claim that $F(q,p,t)=p\sin\omega t+m\omega q\cos\omega t$ is conserved. If it is false, construct two independent explicitly time-dependent invariants and recover $q(t)$ from their constant values.
permittedResults: Keep the explicit time derivative; a vanishing Poisson bracket is not required for a time-dependent invariant.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the explicit time derivative and Poisson bracket of the displayed candidate separately. Next: When they add instead of canceling, construct the two phase-quadrature combinations whose terms cancel. Finally: Evaluate both constants at $t=0$ and reconstruct a solution that satisfies the equation and initial data.
hints: Compute the explicit time derivative and Poisson bracket of the displayed candidate separately.
When they add instead of canceling, construct the two phase-quadrature combinations whose terms cancel.
Evaluate both constants at $t=0$ and reconstruct a solution that satisfies the equation and initial data.
problems.solution: $\partial_tF=\omega p\cos\omega t-m\omega^2q\sin\omega t$. With $\{F,H\}=F_qH_p-F_pH_q$, the Poisson bracket is the same expression, so the two terms add and the claim is false. Instead $A=p\cos\omega t+m\omega q\sin\omega t$ and $B=m\omega q\cos\omega t-p\sin\omega t$ each satisfy $\partial_tA+\{A,H\}=0$ and $\partial_tB+\{B,H\}=0$. At $t=0$, $A=p_0$ and $B=m\omega q_0$. Solving for the coordinate gives $q(t)=[B\cos\omega t+A\sin\omega t]/(m\omega)$, which also satisfies the oscillator equation and initial data.
rubricCriteria: The candidate's explicit derivative and Poisson bracket are computed separately and shown to add.
Two corrected linear combinations cancel under $\partial_t+\{\cdot,H\}$ and reduce to $p_0$ and $m\omega q_0$.
Solving those constants for $q(t)$ recovers both the oscillator equation and initial data.

commonErrors.description: Drops $\partial F/\partial t$ and tests only the Poisson bracket.
commonErrors.consequence: Testing only the Poisson bracket applies an autonomous-observable criterion to a time-dependent function.

commonErrors.description: Declares the displayed candidate conserved even though its two evolution terms add.
commonErrors.consequence: Certifying terms that add instead of cancel makes a changing quantity masquerade as an invariant.

problems.flawedProof: Ignore explicit time dependence and test only the Poisson bracket. Treating the sine and cosine coefficients as irrelevant gives $\{F,H\}=0$, so the displayed $F$ is conserved.

problems.title: Cyclic polar angle in the free-particle Hamiltonian
problems.objective: Construct free-particle Hamiltonian motion in polar canonical variables and interpret its outward radial equation without inventing a force.
problems.statement: A free particle of mass $m$ moves in a plane. Starting from $L=m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2)/2$, derive $p_r$, $p_\theta$, and the Hamiltonian. Use Hamilton's equations to prove $p_\theta$ is constant and derive the radial equation.
permittedResults: The angular velocity is $\dot\theta=p_\theta/(mr^2)$, not $p_\theta/m$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute both momenta from the polar kinetic metric. Next: Invert both rates and form the Legendre transform. Finally: Use the cyclic angle to conserve angular momentum and derive the radial equation.
hints: Compute both momenta from the polar kinetic metric.
Invert both rates and form the Legendre transform.
Use the cyclic angle to conserve angular momentum and derive the radial equation.
problems.solution: $p_r=m\dot r$ and $p_\theta=mr^2\dot\theta$. The Legendre transform gives $H=p_r^2/(2m)+p_\theta^2/(2mr^2)$. Because $H$ is independent of $\theta$, $\dot p_\theta=-\partial H/\partial\theta=0$. The radial equations are $\dot r=p_r/m$ and $\dot p_r=p_\theta^2/(mr^3)$, so $m\ddot r=p_\theta^2/(mr^3)$. The outward radial term is the coordinate expression of straight inertial motion with nonzero angular momentum, not a new physical force.
rubricCriteria: The angular momentum $p_\theta=mr^2\dot\theta$ includes the polar metric factor.
Legendre transformation gives the $p_\theta^2/(2mr^2)$ term and cyclicity conserves $p_\theta$.
The radial Hamilton equations reproduce straight inertial motion and distinguish coordinate acceleration from external force.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p_\theta=m\dot\theta$ and misses the metric factor $r^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing $r^2$ changes angular momentum dimensions and every radial term that follows.

commonErrors.description: Interprets the radial Hamilton equation as evidence of an external centrifugal force in the inertial frame.
commonErrors.consequence: Calling the coordinate centrifugal term an applied inertial-frame force misidentifies free motion.

problems.flawedProof: The free Hamiltonian is $(p_r^2+p_\theta^2)/(2m)$ because polar coordinates are orthonormal.

problems.title: Area preservation by a one-degree Hamiltonian flow
problems.objective: Prove local phase-area preservation from the divergence of a one-pair Hamiltonian vector field under explicit regularity assumptions.
problems.statement: Let $H(q,p)$ be twice continuously differentiable. Prove the phase-plane velocity field $(\dot q,\dot p)=(H_p,-H_q)$ has zero divergence and therefore preserves infinitesimal oriented area. State exactly which equality of mixed derivatives is used.
permittedResults: Compute $\partial\dot q/\partial q+\partial\dot p/\partial p$.
problems.strategy: First: Write the Hamiltonian vector field in the declared coordinate order. Next: Differentiate its two components and invoke equality of continuous mixed partials. Finally: Translate zero divergence into area preservation without claiming distance preservation.
hints: Write the Hamiltonian vector field in the declared coordinate order.
Differentiate its two components and invoke equality of continuous mixed partials.
Translate zero divergence into area preservation without claiming distance preservation.
problems.solution: The divergence is $\partial_qH_p+\partial_p(-H_q)=H_{pq}-H_{qp}=0$. Equality follows from continuity of the second derivatives. For a small material phase-area element, the instantaneous fractional rate of change equals this divergence, so the area is preserved. The result does not say Euclidean distances or the shape of the element are preserved; Hamiltonian shear can distort it while keeping area. If $H$ lacks the regularity needed for equal mixed derivatives, this proof does not apply automatically.
rubricCriteria: The divergence is written as $H_{pq}-H_{qp}$ in the declared $(q,p)$ order.
Continuity of second derivatives justifies equality of the mixed partials.
Zero divergence is translated into area preservation without claiming distance or shape preservation.

commonErrors.description: Computes $H_{pp}-H_{qq}$ as the phase divergence.
commonErrors.consequence: Using pure second derivatives instead of mixed ones does not compute the Hamiltonian-flow divergence.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that every phase-space shape moves by a rigid rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: Area-preserving shear can deform shapes, so rigid-motion conclusions exceed Liouville's result.

problems.flawedProof: The phase divergence is $H_{pp}-H_{qq}$, which vanishes for every Hamiltonian because the two second derivatives are equal.

problems.title: Canonical scaling of an oscillator
problems.objective: Choose a reciprocal canonical scaling that renders oscillator coordinate and momentum coefficients symmetric while tracking units and invertibility.
problems.statement: For nonzero constant $\alpha$, define $Q=\alpha q$ and $P=p/\alpha$. Prove the map is canonical, transform $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, and choose $\alpha=\sqrt{m\omega}$ to obtain symmetric dimensionless coefficients. State the units carried by $Q$ and $P$.
permittedResults: Check $\{Q,P\}_{q,p}=1$ before transforming the Hamiltonian.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the elementary Poisson brackets and invert the map. Next: Substitute the inverse variables into both Hamiltonian terms. Finally: Choose the scale that equalizes coefficients and audit invertibility and units.
hints: Compute the elementary Poisson brackets and invert the map.
Substitute the inverse variables into both Hamiltonian terms.
Choose the scale that equalizes coefficients and audit invertibility and units.
problems.solution: $\{Q,P\}=\alpha(1/\alpha)=1$, with the other elementary brackets zero, so the map is canonical. Since $q=Q/\alpha$ and $p=\alpha P$, $H=\alpha^2P^2/(2m)+m\omega^2Q^2/(2\alpha^2)$. For $\alpha=\sqrt{m\omega}$, $H=\omega(P^2+Q^2)/2$. Then $Q$ and $P$ each have square-root-of-action units, and their product has action units. The singular choice $\alpha=0$ is excluded because it is not invertible.
rubricCriteria: The bracket $\{\alpha q,p/\alpha\}=1$ verifies canonical reciprocity.
Substitution produces coefficients $\alpha^2/m$ and $m\omega^2/\alpha^2$ before they are balanced.
The choice $\sqrt{m\omega}$ gives square-root-of-action variables and excludes the singular zero scale.

commonErrors.description: Scales both $q$ and $p$ by the same factor and calls the map canonical.
commonErrors.consequence: Scaling both canonical variables in the same direction multiplies phase area by $\alpha^2$.

commonErrors.description: Chooses $\alpha=0$ to remove one Hamiltonian term.
commonErrors.consequence: A zero scale destroys invertibility, so it cannot be used to simplify a canonical Hamiltonian.

problems.flawedProof: Any linear rescaling is canonical, so $Q=\alpha q$ and $P=\alpha p$ works.

problems.title: Momentum shear from a type-2 generating function
problems.objective: Extract a momentum shear from a type-2 generator, transform a natural Hamiltonian, and confirm the map by its fundamental bracket.
problems.statement: Let $F_2(q,P)=qP+\alpha q^2/2$. Derive the canonical transformation. Apply it to $H=p^2/(2m)+V(q)$ and write the transformed Hamiltonian $K(Q,P)$. Verify the map by a Poisson bracket.
permittedResults: For a type-2 generator, $p=\partial F_2/\partial q$ and $Q=\partial F_2/\partial P$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the type-2 generator with respect to its two declared variables. Next: Invert the shear and substitute it into the old Hamiltonian. Finally: Check the fundamental bracket and the identity limit.
hints: Differentiate the type-2 generator with respect to its two declared variables.
Invert the shear and substitute it into the old Hamiltonian.
Check the fundamental bracket and the identity limit.
problems.solution: $p=P+\alpha q$ and $Q=q$, so the inverse is $q=Q$, $p=P+\alpha Q$. Because the generator is time independent, $K=H=(P+\alpha Q)^2/(2m)+V(Q)$. Directly, $\{Q,P\}_{q,p}=\{q,p-\alpha q\}=1$. The transformation shears momentum while preserving phase area. At $\alpha=0$ it reduces to the identity.
rubricCriteria: Generator derivatives give $p=P+\alpha q$ and $Q=q$ with the inverse sign handled correctly.
The transformed kinetic energy is $(P+\alpha Q)^2/(2m)$ because the generator is time independent.
A direct bracket check and the $\alpha=0$ limit verify canonical structure.

commonErrors.description: Uses $P=p+\alpha q$ instead of solving $p=P+\alpha q$.
commonErrors.consequence: Failing to solve the momentum relation reverses the shear and changes the transformed kinetic cross term.

commonErrors.description: Adds $\partial F_2/\partial t$ even though the generator has no time dependence.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonexistent explicit-time term would add spurious energy and alter Hamilton's equations.

problems.flawedProof: From $p=P+\alpha q$, conclude $P=p+\alpha q$ without solving the equation. Thus $Q=q$ and the transformed kinetic term is $(P-\alpha Q)^2/(2m)$.

problems.title: A canonical chart that is locally invertible but globally two-to-one
problems.objective: Separate local symplecticity from global invertibility for a nonlinear canonical chart and track a free trajectory near its excluded boundary.
problems.statement: On the punctured phase plane $q\ne0$, define $Q=q^2/2$ and $P=p/q$. Prove that the map is symplectic, but show that it is globally two-to-one when both signs of $q$ are admitted. Give its inverse on each connected half-plane, construct a type-2 generating function, and transform $H=p^2/(2m)$. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q=-2.00\,\mathrm m$, and $p=3.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, evaluate $(Q,P)$, $K$, $\dot Q$, and $\dot P$ in the new chart. Explain what happens when the free trajectory crosses $q=0$.
permittedResults: A unit fundamental Poisson bracket proves local symplecticity, but it does not by itself prove global one-to-one behavior.
problems.strategy: First: Check the fundamental bracket and compare points related by simultaneous sign reversal. Next: invert the map separately on the positive and negative half-planes and derive its generator. Finally: transform the Hamiltonian, evaluate the numerical event, and interpret the coordinate singularity at the omitted line.
hints: Compare the images of $(q,p)$ and $(-q,-p)$ after evaluating $\{Q,P\}$.
On either branch, $q=\pm\sqrt{2Q}$ and $p=qP$.
Use $F_2=q^2P/2$ and compare Hamilton's equations for $K$ with direct differentiation of $Q$ and $P$.
problems.solution: The bracket is $\{Q,P\}=q(1/q)=1$, and in fact $P\,dQ=(p/q)q\,dq=p\,dq$, so the map is locally symplectic. Yet $(q,p)$ and $(-q,-p)$ have the same $(Q,P)$, making the full punctured-plane map two-to-one. On $q>0$ or $q<0$ separately, the inverse is $q=\pm\sqrt{2Q}$ and $p=qP$. A type-2 generator is $F_2=q^2P/2$, because $p=\partial_qF_2=qP$ and $Q=\partial_PF_2=q^2/2$. Thus $K=QP^2/m$. The data give $Q=2.00\,\mathrm{m^2}$, $P=-1.50\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, and $K=2.25\,\mathrm J$, equal to $p^2/(2m)$. Hamilton's equations give $\dot Q=2QP/m=-3.00\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ and $\dot P=-P^2/m=-1.125\,\mathrm{kg/s^2}$, matching direct differentiation. A crossing of $q=0$ is regular free motion but reaches $Q=0$, where this chart is singular and must be replaced or switched between branches.
rubricCriteria: The unit bracket and canonical one-form prove local symplecticity, while simultaneous sign reversal proves the full map is two-to-one.
Branchwise inversion and $F_2=q^2P/2$ reproduce both transformation equations and $K=QP^2/m$.
The numerical phase point, energy, and time derivatives are correct, and the regular physical crossing is distinguished from the chart singularity.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that $\{Q,P\}=1$ makes the map a global canonical diffeomorphism on the entire punctured plane.
commonErrors.consequence: The local bracket test cannot detect the two-to-one identification of $(q,p)$ with $(-q,-p)$.

commonErrors.description: Uses only $q=+\sqrt{2Q}$ and treats it as a global inverse.
commonErrors.consequence: Discarding the negative branch loses half the phase space and gives the wrong continuation through a chart change.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\{Q,P\}=1$, the map is automatically a one-to-one canonical transformation on all $q\ne0$. The inverse is globally $q=+\sqrt{2Q}$ and $p=P\sqrt{2Q}$.

problems.title: Time-dependent translation of a free-particle Hamiltonian
problems.objective: Transform free-particle motion to a uniformly translating coordinate through a time-dependent generator and reconcile both frames.
problems.statement: A free particle has $H=p^2/(2m)$. Use $F_2(q,P,t)=(q-vt)P$ to transform to $Q=q-vt$. Derive $p$, $Q$, and the new Hamiltonian. Obtain Hamilton's equations and reconcile them with inertial free motion. State the error caused by omitting $\partial F_2/\partial t$.
permittedResults: For a time-dependent type-2 generator, $K=H+\partial F_2/\partial t$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the generating function with respect to both canonical variables. Next: Include its explicit time derivative before applying Hamilton's equations. Finally: Transform the resulting motion back to the inertial coordinate and check the zero-speed limit.
hints: Differentiate the generating function with respect to both canonical variables.
Include its explicit time derivative before applying Hamilton's equations.
Transform the resulting motion back to the inertial coordinate and check the zero-speed limit.
problems.solution: $p=P$ and $Q=q-vt$. The explicit derivative is $-vP$, so $K=P^2/(2m)-vP$. Hamilton's equations give $\dot Q=P/m-v$ and $\dot P=0$. Since $q=Q+vt$, $\dot q=P/m$ and $\ddot q=0$, as required. Omitting the time term would give $\dot Q=P/m$, inconsistent with differentiating the declared coordinate transformation. At $v=0$ the original Hamiltonian returns.
rubricCriteria: Generator derivatives yield $Q=q-vt$ and unchanged canonical momentum $p=P$.
The explicit derivative contributes $-vP$ to the new Hamiltonian.
New equations transform back to $\ddot q=0$ and reduce to the original Hamiltonian at $v=0$.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes variables into $H$ but drops the generator's explicit time derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping the generator's time derivative predicts a coordinate velocity incompatible with differentiating $Q=q-vt$.

commonErrors.description: Changes the momentum by $mv$ even though the stated generator gives $p=P$.
commonErrors.consequence: Adding $mv$ to momentum describes a different canonical map from the one generated here.

problems.flawedProof: The new Hamiltonian remains $P^2/(2m)$ because canonical transformations never add time terms.

problems.title: Hamiltonian in a uniformly rotating plane
problems.objective: Derive the rotating-plane Hamiltonian and eliminate canonical momentum to recover Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations with one consistent sign convention.
problems.statement: A particle moves in a planar potential $V(x,y)$ that is stationary in a frame rotating at constant $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\mathbf e_z$. Derive the rotating-frame Hamiltonian $K=(p_x^2+p_y^2)/(2m)+V-\Omega L_z$, where $L_z=xp_y-yp_x$. Derive the velocity-momentum relation and the second-order rotating-frame equation. Identify the conserved quantity.
permittedResults: Apply Hamilton's equations to $K$ before eliminating canonical momentum.
problems.strategy: First: Use the canonical angular-momentum term with its declared sign. Next: Derive both first-order equations and eliminate momentum carefully. Finally: Identify Coriolis, centrifugal, and the time-independent conserved Hamiltonian.
hints: Use the canonical angular-momentum term with its declared sign.
Derive both first-order equations and eliminate momentum carefully.
Identify Coriolis, centrifugal, and the time-independent conserved Hamiltonian.
problems.solution: Hamilton's equations give $\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf p/m-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$, so $\mathbf p=m(\dot{\mathbf r}+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$. The momentum equation is $\dot{\mathbf p}=-\nabla V-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf p$. Differentiation and elimination produce $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\nabla V-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\dot{\mathbf r}-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$. The two extra terms are Coriolis and centrifugal contributions with the declared rotating-coordinate convention. Because $K$ has no explicit time dependence, $K$ is conserved; it is the rotating-frame Jacobi energy, not generally the inertial energy.
rubricCriteria: The $-\Omega L_z$ coupling leads to $\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf p/m-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$.
Momentum elimination yields both $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ and $-\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$.
Autonomy identifies the rotating Jacobi energy while distinguishing it from inertial energy.

commonErrors.description: Treats canonical momentum as $m\dot{\mathbf r}$ in rotating coordinates.
commonErrors.consequence: Equating canonical and mechanical momentum in rotating coordinates removes the velocity shift and corrupts both fictitious terms.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+\Omega L_z$ while retaining equations for the opposite rotation convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the angular-momentum coupling sign without changing rotation convention reverses Coriolis dynamics.

problems.flawedProof: Rotation changes only the potential; there is no momentum coupling in the Hamiltonian.

problems.title: Energy diagnostic for a translating harmonic trap
problems.objective: Diagnose energy exchange with a translating harmonic trap using the explicit-time Hamiltonian identity and a signed numerical power.
problems.statement: Prove along Hamiltonian motion that $dH/dt=\partial H/\partial t$. Apply it to a translating harmonic trap $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2[q-a(t)]^2/2$ with $a(t)=A\sin(\nu t)$. Derive the equation of motion and exact power transferred to the particle. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\omega=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $A=0.200\,\mathrm m$, $\nu=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and instantaneous $q=0.150\,\mathrm m$ at $t=0$, find $dH/dt$ and interpret its sign.
permittedResults: Expand the total derivative and use both Hamilton equations.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the Hamiltonian along a trajectory without assuming autonomy. Next: Cancel the canonical terms, then derive the moving-center equation and explicit-time power. Finally: Evaluate the signed power with SI units and check both stationary-trap limits.
hints: Differentiate the Hamiltonian along a trajectory without assuming autonomy.
Cancel the canonical terms, then derive the moving-center equation and explicit-time power.
Evaluate the signed power with SI units and check both stationary-trap limits.
problems.solution:
$dH/dt=H_q\dot q+H_p\dot p+H_t=H_qH_p+H_p(-H_q)+H_t=H_t$. Hamilton's equations give $\ddot q+\omega^2[q-a(t)]=0$. The exact power is $H_t=-m\omega^2[q-a(t)]\dot a(t)$, where $\dot a=A
u\cos(
u t)$. At $t=0$, $a=0$ and $\dot a=0.800\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $dH/dt=-2(3)^2(0.150)(0.800)=-2.16\,\mathrm W$. The negative sign means the moving support is instantaneously removing modeled particle energy for the stated displacement and direction. As $A	o0$ or $
u	o0$, the trap becomes stationary and the power vanishes.
rubricCriteria: Canonical terms cancel only after leaving $H_t$, proving $dH/dt=\partial H/\partial t$.
The moving-center equation and power $-m\omega^2(q-a)\dot a$ follow from the same Hamiltonian.
The initial data give $-2.16$ W, with physical sign interpretation and both stationary-trap limits.

commonErrors.description: Concludes every Hamiltonian is conserved because the canonical terms cancel.
commonErrors.consequence: Canonical cancellation does not remove explicit parameter power, so declaring universal conservation ignores the moving support.

commonErrors.description: Sets the rate to zero whenever the particle has zero instantaneous velocity, ignoring motion of the trap.
commonErrors.consequence: Particle velocity can vanish while the trap moves and changes stored potential energy, so zero particle speed does not imply zero power.

problems.flawedProof: The two canonical terms cancel, so $dH/dt=0$ for every Hamiltonian, including a translating trap; explicit time dependence cannot change that conclusion.

problems.title: Poisson algebra of orbital angular momentum
problems.objective: Recover the orbital-angular-momentum Poisson algebra and verify its action as the signed generator of active rotations.
problems.statement: In three canonical dimensions let $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p$. Prove $\{L_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $\{r_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}r_k$. Use the second identity to interpret $L_j$ as the generator of infinitesimal rotations.
permittedResults: Write $L_i=\epsilon_{iab}r_ap_b$ and use the elementary canonical brackets.
problems.strategy: First: Expand angular momentum with the Levi-Civita symbol and elementary brackets. Next: Contract the Kronecker deltas and reduce the epsilon products. Finally: Check one component against the declared active-rotation convention and explain the generator action.
hints: Expand angular momentum with the Levi-Civita symbol and elementary brackets.
Contract the Kronecker deltas and reduce the epsilon products.
Check one component against the declared active-rotation convention and explain the generator action.
problems.solution: Expanding with $\{r_a,p_b\}=\delta_{ab}$ gives $\{r_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{jai}r_a=\epsilon_{ijk}r_k$ after a cyclic index relabeling. Thus $\delta r_i=\varepsilon\{r_i,L_j\}=\varepsilon\epsilon_{ijk}r_k$. A parallel expansion of both factors in $L_i$ and $L_j$ yields $\{L_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$; in particular $\{L_x,L_y\}=L_z$. With the declared rule $\delta f=\varepsilon\{f,L_z\}$, one finds $\delta x=-\varepsilon y$ and $\delta y=\varepsilon x$, the standard positive active rotation about $z$. Antisymmetry supplies every reversed bracket.
rubricCriteria: Levi-Civita expansion gives $\{r_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}r_k$ with contracted indices shown.
A parallel calculation produces $\{L_i,L_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$.
The $z$-rotation test sends $\delta x=-\varepsilon y$ and $\delta y=\varepsilon x$, fixing convention signs.

commonErrors.description: Treats angular-momentum components as mutually commuting constants.
commonErrors.consequence: Ordinary product commutativity does not imply vanishing canonical derivatives, so zero angular-momentum brackets are false.

commonErrors.description: Quotes the Lie algebra without checking the active-generator sign convention.
commonErrors.consequence: An untested quoted algebra can carry the opposite active/passive sign and generate the wrong rotation.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf p$ commute as ordinary products, every Poisson bracket of $L_i$ vanishes.

problems.title: Hamiltonian reduction of an inverse-square central force
problems.objective: Reduce inverse-square motion Hamiltonianly and identify zero linear apsidal precession through the radial symplectic flow over one orbit.
problems.statement: For reduced mass $\mu$ in $V(r)=-k/r$ with $k>0$, derive the planar polar Hamiltonian, reduce it using conserved angular momentum $L>0$, and find the circular radius, circular energy, and orbital angular frequency. Linearize the canonical radial pair $(r,p_r)$ about the circular orbit, find its Hamiltonian matrix and eigenvalues, and prove the radial frequency equals the orbital frequency. Evaluate the one-orbit linear radial map.
permittedResults: Use $H=p_r^2/(2\mu)+p_\theta^2/(2\mu r^2)-k/r$ and set $p_\theta=L$.
problems.strategy: First: Construct the polar Hamiltonian and identify the cyclic angle. Next: Find the circular fixed point and linearize both canonical radial Hamilton equations there. Finally: Compare the symplectic eigenfrequency with orbital motion and evaluate the full-period matrix exponential.
hints: Construct the polar Hamiltonian and identify the cyclic angle.
Find the circular fixed point and linearize both canonical radial Hamilton equations there.
Compare the symplectic eigenfrequency with orbital motion and evaluate the full-period matrix exponential.
problems.solution: The reduced Hamiltonian is $H_r=p_r^2/(2\mu)+U_{eff}$ with $U_{eff}=L^2/(2\mu r^2)-k/r$. The condition $U_{eff}'=0$ gives $r_c=L^2/(\mu k)$ and $E_c=-k/(2r_c)=-\mu k^2/(2L^2)$. The orbital rate satisfies $\Omega=L/(\mu r_c^2)$ and $\Omega^2=k/(\mu r_c^3)$. Since $U_{eff}''(r_c)=k/r_c^3$, the perturbation vector $(\delta r,\delta p_r)^{\mathsf T}$ obeys $\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=A\boldsymbol\xi$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\mu\\-k/r_c^3&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $\pm i\sqrt{k/(\mu r_c^3)}=\pm i\Omega$. Over one circular period $2\pi/\Omega$, $e^{A(2\pi/\Omega)}=\mathbf1$, the linear no-apsidal-precession signature of the inverse-square potential.
rubricCriteria: The conserved polar momentum creates the effective potential and fixes $r_c=L^2/(\mu k)$ and $E_c$.
Linearizing $(r,p_r)$ gives the displayed Hamiltonian matrix with eigenvalues $\pm i\Omega$.
Its exponential over $2\pi/\Omega$ is the identity, matching the independently computed orbital frequency.

commonErrors.description: Minimizes the bare potential instead of the angular-momentum effective potential.
commonErrors.consequence: The bare attractive potential has no finite minimum; omitting the angular barrier cannot produce the circular orbit.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p_\theta=\mu\dot\theta$ and misses $r^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing the polar $r^2$ factor changes the conserved angular momentum and destroys the frequency comparison.

problems.flawedProof: The circular radius follows from $-k/r$ alone and therefore does not depend on angular momentum.

problems.title: Symplectic test for a linear phase map
problems.objective: Apply the full symplectic matrix test to a concrete linear map and cross-check it through inversion and a Poisson bracket.
problems.statement: Let $(Q,P)^{\mathsf T}=M(q,p)^{\mathsf T}$ with $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Verify $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$ for $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find the inverse map and check $\{Q,P\}=1$ directly.
permittedResults: For a two-dimensional linear map, the symplectic condition is equivalent to determinant one, but verify the full matrix identity.
problems.strategy: First: Compute determinant and the complete $M^{\mathsf T}JM$ product. Next: Invert the matrix using its unit determinant. Finally: Evaluate the fundamental bracket and compare with a nearby noncanonical matrix.
hints: Compute determinant and the complete $M^{\mathsf T}JM$ product.
Invert the matrix using its unit determinant.
Evaluate the fundamental bracket and compare with a nearby noncanonical matrix.
problems.solution: $\det M=2(1)-1(1)=1$. Direct multiplication gives $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$. The inverse is $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, so $q=Q-P$ and $p=-Q+2P$. Directly, $\{Q,P\}=Q_qP_p-Q_pP_q=2(1)-1(1)=1$. Thus the map is globally invertible and canonical. Replacing the lower-right entry by $2$ would make determinant three and fail the test.
rubricCriteria: Direct multiplication verifies $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$ rather than relying on matrix symmetry.
The inverse map is computed using the unit determinant.
The component bracket $2(1)-1(1)$ equals one and agrees with the matrix criterion.

commonErrors.description: Checks only that $M$ is symmetric and calls symmetry equivalent to symplecticity.
commonErrors.consequence: Symmetric matrices need not preserve the canonical two-form, so symmetry is not a substitute for the $J$ test.

commonErrors.description: Uses $M^{\mathsf T}M=I$ as the canonical condition.
commonErrors.consequence: Orthogonality preserves Euclidean length, not necessarily symplectic area; $M^{\mathsf T}M=I$ is the wrong condition.

problems.flawedProof: The matrix $M$ is symmetric, and every symmetric linear map is symplectic. Therefore no $M^{\mathsf T}JM$ or Poisson-bracket calculation is needed.

problems.title: Infinitesimal canonical scaling generated by $qp$
problems.objective: Integrate the Poisson flow generated by $qp$ from its infinitesimal action to an exact reciprocal scaling.
problems.statement: Let $G(q,p)=qp$ and define an infinitesimal transformation by $\delta f=\varepsilon\{f,G\}$. Find $\delta q$ and $\delta p$, integrate the generator flow to a finite transformation, and verify the finite map preserves $dq\wedge dp$.
permittedResults: Treat the group parameter as an evolution variable generated by $G$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute both elementary brackets with the generator. Next: Integrate the parameter-flow equations rather than truncating permanently at first order. Finally: Check the exact wedge product or Poisson bracket of the finite map.
hints: Compute both elementary brackets with the generator.
Integrate the parameter-flow equations rather than truncating permanently at first order.
Check the exact wedge product or Poisson bracket of the finite map.
problems.solution: $\{q,G\}=q$ and $\{p,G\}=-p$, so $dq/ds=q$ and $dp/ds=-p$ along the generator flow. Hence $Q=e^s q$ and $P=e^{-s}p$. The product differential satisfies $dQ\wedge dP=e^se^{-s}dq\wedge dp=dq\wedge dp$, and $\{Q,P\}=1$. To first order, $Q=(1+\varepsilon)q$ and $P=(1-\varepsilon)p$. Scaling both variables in the same direction would change area.
rubricCriteria: The generator gives opposite infinitesimal signs for coordinate and momentum.
Parameter-flow integration yields $Q=e^sq$ and $P=e^{-s}p$.
The wedge product and fundamental bracket remain unchanged, with the first-order limit recovered.

commonErrors.description: Gives the same positive scaling to both $q$ and $p$.
commonErrors.consequence: Scaling both variables upward changes phase area instead of generating a canonical dilation.

commonErrors.description: Treats the infinitesimal parameter as physical time without specifying a Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: The group parameter labels a canonical transformation and is not physical time unless a Hamiltonian evolution is separately specified.

problems.flawedProof: The generator $qp$ produces $Q=e^sq$ and $P=e^sp$, which is canonical because their product is unchanged.

problems.title: Poisson brackets transported by Hamiltonian flow
problems.objective: Use the Jacobi identity to prove Poisson brackets are transported consistently by autonomous Hamiltonian flow.
problems.statement: For time-independent observables $f$ and $g$ and autonomous Hamiltonian $H$, prove $d\{f,g\}/dt=\{\dot f,g\}+\{f,\dot g\}=\{\{f,g\},H\}$. State the Jacobi identity step and explain why an initially canonical pair remains canonical.
permittedResults: Use $\dot f=\{f,H\}$ and the Jacobi identity with the ordered triple $(f,g,H)$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the bracket using bilinearity and the derivative rule. Next: Apply the Jacobi identity with a fixed argument order to combine the nested brackets. Finally: Apply the result to initial brackets one and zero, noting the time-dependent caveat.
hints: Differentiate the bracket using bilinearity and the derivative rule.
Apply the Jacobi identity with a fixed argument order to combine the nested brackets.
Apply the result to initial brackets one and zero, noting the time-dependent caveat.
problems.solution: The derivative property gives $\{\dot f,g\}+\{f,\dot g\}=\{\{f,H\},g\}+\{f,\{g,H\}\}$. Jacobi identity rearranges this sum to $\{\{f,g\},H\}$. Thus the bracket itself evolves as an observable. If initially $\{f,g\}=1$, the right side is $\{1,H\}=0$, so the bracket stays one. Likewise zero elementary brackets remain zero. This is the local canonical character of Hamiltonian flow. Explicitly time-dependent observables require their partial-time terms as well.
rubricCriteria: Time differentiation is distributed over both bracket arguments using their Hamilton equations.
The ordered Jacobi identity combines the nested terms into $\{\{f,g\},H\}$.
Initial brackets one and zero remain so, while explicitly time-dependent observables are correctly excluded.

commonErrors.description: Assumes nested Poisson brackets are associative.
commonErrors.consequence: Poisson brackets are not associative, so reassociating nested brackets invalidates the transport proof.

commonErrors.description: Concludes every bracket is constant rather than only brackets whose bracket with $H$ vanishes.
commonErrors.consequence: Only a bracket commuting with $H$ is constant; the transport equation does not freeze every observable bracket.

problems.flawedProof: Treat nested Poisson brackets as associative: $\{\{f,H\},g\}=\{f,\{H,g\}\}$. The two derivative terms therefore cancel directly, so every Poisson bracket is constant.

problems.title: Liouville theorem in $2n$-dimensional phase space
problems.objective: Extend Liouville's divergence cancellation to $2n$ canonical dimensions and distinguish volume preservation from energy conservation.
problems.statement: For canonical coordinates $(q_i,p_i)_{i=1}^n$ and a $C^2$ Hamiltonian, compute the divergence of the Hamiltonian vector field and prove phase-volume preservation. Explain why the result survives explicit time dependence of $H$ at each fixed time.
permittedResults: Sum $\partial\dot q_i/\partial q_i+\partial\dot p_i/\partial p_i$ over all canonical pairs.
problems.strategy: First: Write the full canonical vector field and its divergence. Next: Pair each mixed derivative with its cancelling transpose. Finally: Distinguish phase-volume preservation from energy conservation for time-dependent Hamiltonians.
hints: Write the full canonical vector field and its divergence.
Pair each mixed derivative with its cancelling transpose.
Distinguish phase-volume preservation from energy conservation for time-dependent Hamiltonians.
problems.solution: Hamilton's equations give divergence $\sum_i[\partial_{q_i}H_{p_i}+\partial_{p_i}(-H_{q_i})]=\sum_i(H_{p_iq_i}-H_{q_ip_i})=0$. A material phase volume therefore has zero instantaneous logarithmic rate of change, so the flow Jacobian determinant remains one when it starts at one. If $H$ depends explicitly on time, the same mixed-partial cancellation holds for the vector field at each time; autonomy is not required for volume preservation. Energy conservation, by contrast, can fail when $H_t\ne0$.
rubricCriteria: Each canonical pair contributes equal mixed derivatives with opposite signs.
Zero total divergence implies a unit flow-Jacobian determinant for material phase volume.
The cancellation is shown to survive explicit time dependence even when energy does not.

commonErrors.description: Adds all second derivatives instead of pairing mixed partials.
commonErrors.consequence: Adding rather than cancelling mixed derivatives produces a fictitious compressibility of Hamiltonian flow.

commonErrors.description: Claims explicit time dependence destroys symplectic volume preservation.
commonErrors.consequence: Explicit time dependence can change energy but does not alter the equal-time symplectic divergence identity.

problems.flawedProof: Add the mixed derivatives instead of subtracting them: the divergence is $\sum_i(H_{p_iq_i}+H_{q_ip_i})$. It vanishes only for autonomous Hamiltonians with conserved energy.

problems.title: Phase area enclosed by the pendulum separatrix
problems.objective: Integrate both momentum branches of the pendulum separatrix to obtain its exact enclosed phase area and action dimensions.
problems.statement: A plane pendulum has $H=p^2/(2m\ell^2)+mg\ell(1-\cos q)$. At the separatrix energy $E_s=2mg\ell$, find the upper branch $p_+(q)$ for $-\pi\le q\le\pi$ and compute the exact phase-space area inside the separatrix. State its units.
permittedResults: Use $1+\cos q=2\cos^2(q/2)$ on the stated interval.
