problems.strategy: First: Solve the separatrix energy equation for both momentum branches. Next: Use the half-angle identity and integrate their vertical separation. Finally: Check endpoint zeros and angular-action dimensions.
hints: Solve the separatrix energy equation for both momentum branches.
Use the half-angle identity and integrate their vertical separation.
Check endpoint zeros and angular-action dimensions.
problems.solution: At $E_s$, $p^2/(2m\ell^2)=mg\ell(1+\cos q)=2mg\ell\cos^2(q/2)$. Thus $p_+(q)=2m\ell\sqrt{g\ell}\cos(q/2)$ and the lower branch is its negative. The enclosed area is $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}[p_+-p_-]dq=4m\ell\sqrt{g\ell}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(q/2)dq=16m\ell\sqrt{g\ell}$. Momentum times dimensionless angle has angular-action units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. The branch vanishes at both unstable endpoints.
rubricCriteria: At $E_s$, the half-angle identity yields $p_+=2m\ell\sqrt{g\ell}\cos(q/2)$ on the full interval.
Upper-minus-lower integration gives $16m\ell\sqrt{g\ell}$.
Endpoint zeros and angular-action units independently check the result.

commonErrors.description: Integrates only the upper branch and misses the lower half of the lobe.
commonErrors.consequence: Integrating only one branch returns half the enclosed lobe area.

commonErrors.description: Uses $1-\cos q$ after moving the potential to the other side at separatrix energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Using the unmoved potential sign changes the separatrix branch and fails to vanish at the unstable endpoints.

problems.flawedProof: The area is $2\pi E_s$ because every periodic orbit has area equal to energy times period.

problems.title: Canonical normal modes of two coupled oscillators
problems.objective: Diagonalize two coupled oscillators with one orthogonal transformation applied canonically to both coordinates and momenta.
problems.statement: For unit masses consider $H=(p_1^2+p_2^2)/2+\omega_0^2(q_1^2+q_2^2)/2+\kappa(q_1-q_2)^2/2$, with $\omega_0>0$ and $\kappa\ge0$. Construct canonical symmetric and antisymmetric coordinates, diagonalize $H$, and find both frequencies. Verify the transformation is symplectic.
permittedResults: Use the same orthogonal matrix on coordinates and momenta.
problems.strategy: First: Choose orthonormal symmetry coordinates and transform momenta with the identical matrix. Next: Substitute into kinetic and potential terms and collect independent modes. Finally: Check elementary brackets and the zero-coupling degeneracy.
hints: Choose orthonormal symmetry coordinates and transform momenta with the identical matrix.
Substitute into kinetic and potential terms and collect independent modes.
Check elementary brackets and the zero-coupling degeneracy.
problems.solution: Define $Q_+=(q_1+q_2)/\sqrt2$, $Q_-=(q_1-q_2)/\sqrt2$, and similarly $P_\pm=(p_1\pm p_2)/\sqrt2$. Applying one orthogonal matrix to both halves preserves all elementary brackets. The Hamiltonian becomes $H=[P_+^2+\omega_0^2Q_+^2]/2+[P_-^2+(\omega_0^2+2\kappa)Q_-^2]/2$. Thus $\omega_+=\omega_0$ and $\omega_-=\sqrt{\omega_0^2+2\kappa}$. At $\kappa=0$ the frequencies become degenerate, while the canonical transformation remains valid.
rubricCriteria: Symmetric and antisymmetric variables are normalized by the same orthogonal matrix in both phase-space halves.
The transformed Hamiltonian separates into frequencies $\omega_0$ and $\sqrt{\omega_0^2+2\kappa}$.
Elementary brackets verify the map and the zero-coupling degeneracy is handled correctly.

commonErrors.description: Transforms coordinates but leaves momenta unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: Leaving momenta untransformed breaks the canonical one-form and leaves cross terms in the kinetic energy.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the coupling stiffness to the symmetric mode.
commonErrors.consequence: The coupling depends on $q_1-q_2$, so assigning its stiffness to the symmetric mode reverses the mode physics.

problems.flawedProof: Transform only the coordinates to $Q_\pm=(q_1\pm q_2)/\sqrt2$ but leave $p_1,p_2$ unchanged. The potential is diagonal, so this incomplete map is canonical and both mode frequencies increase by $\kappa$.

problems.title: Canonical completion of a mixed quadratic Hamiltonian
problems.objective: Complete a mixed quadratic Hamiltonian by a canonical momentum shear and classify elliptic, marginal, and hyperbolic cases.
problems.statement: Let $H=(ap^2+2bpq+cq^2)/2$ with real constants, $a>0$. Use a canonical momentum shear to remove the mixed term, derive the oscillation frequency, and state the positive-definiteness condition. Check what happens at $ac-b^2=0$.
permittedResults: Complete the square in momentum using $P=p+(b/a)q$, $Q=q$.
problems.strategy: First: Complete the square while tracking the inverse momentum shear. Next: Verify the shear bracket and derive the reduced Hamilton equations. Finally: Classify positive, zero, and negative determinant cases.
hints: Complete the square while tracking the inverse momentum shear.
Verify the shear bracket and derive the reduced Hamilton equations.
Classify positive, zero, and negative determinant cases.
problems.solution: Set $Q=q$ and $P=p+(b/a)q$, so the inverse is $q=Q$ and $p=P-(b/a)Q$. The map is canonical because $\{Q,P\}=1$. Substitution gives $H=aP^2/2+[c-b^2/a]Q^2/2$. Hamilton's equations yield $\ddot Q+(ac-b^2)Q=0$, so $\omega=\sqrt{ac-b^2}$ when $ac-b^2>0$. Together with $a>0$, this is exactly positive definiteness. At $ac-b^2=0$, the restoring term vanishes and $Q$ drifts rather than oscillates; for a negative value the equilibrium is hyperbolic.
rubricCriteria: The shear $P=p+(b/a)q$ is inverted with the sign needed to cancel $pq$.
The reduced coefficients give $\omega^2=ac-b^2$.
Positive definiteness, zero restoring curvature, and negative determinant are classified separately.

commonErrors.description: Uses a coordinate shear that does not cancel the stated $pq$ term.
commonErrors.consequence: A coordinate shear aimed at the wrong phase variable leaves the mixed term and cannot support the claimed frequency.

commonErrors.description: Calls $a>0$ alone sufficient for a stable positive quadratic Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: Positive kinetic coefficient alone does not control the potential direction; $ac-b^2$ must also be positive.

problems.flawedProof: Use the coordinate shear $Q=q+(b/a)p$, $P=p$. It removes the mixed term and gives frequency $\sqrt{ac+b^2}$ because the cross term always strengthens confinement.

problems.title: Canonical versus mechanical momentum in a magnetic field
problems.objective: Separate canonical and mechanical momentum for electromagnetic coupling and track both under a gauge transformation.
problems.statement: For charge $e$ in electromagnetic potentials, start from $L=m\dot{\mathbf r}^2/2+e\mathbf A(\mathbf r,t)\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}-e\Phi(\mathbf r,t)$. Derive canonical momentum and the Hamiltonian. Under $\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$, $\Phi'=\Phi-\partial_t\chi$, determine how canonical and mechanical momentum transform.
permittedResults: Invert $\mathbf p=m\dot{\mathbf r}+e\mathbf A$ before taking the Legendre transform.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the velocity-dependent Lagrangian to identify canonical momentum. Next: Invert for velocity and complete the Legendre transform. Finally: Apply the gauge transformation to both potentials and distinguish canonical from mechanical momentum.
hints: Differentiate the velocity-dependent Lagrangian to identify canonical momentum.
Invert for velocity and complete the Legendre transform.
Apply the gauge transformation to both potentials and distinguish canonical from mechanical momentum.
problems.solution: $\mathbf p=m\dot{\mathbf r}+e\mathbf A$ while mechanical momentum is $\boldsymbol\pi=m\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf p-e\mathbf A$. The Hamiltonian is $H=(\mathbf p-e\mathbf A)^2/(2m)+e\Phi$. A gauge change adds $e\nabla\chi$ to canonical momentum, so $\mathbf p'=\mathbf p+e\nabla\chi$, but $\boldsymbol\pi'=\mathbf p'-e\mathbf A'=\boldsymbol\pi$. The Hamiltonian representative changes consistently with the time-dependent canonical gauge map, while the Lorentz-force trajectory is unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Differentiating the velocity-dependent Lagrangian gives $\mathbf p=m\dot{\mathbf r}+e\mathbf A$.
The Legendre transform produces minimal coupling $(\mathbf p-e\mathbf A)^2/(2m)+e\Phi$.
Canonical momentum shifts by $e\nabla\chi$ while mechanical momentum and the Lorentz trajectory remain invariant.

commonErrors.description: Identifies canonical momentum with $m\dot{\mathbf r}$ in every gauge.
commonErrors.consequence: Equating canonical with mechanical momentum removes the vector-potential coupling and makes the result gauge dependent.

commonErrors.description: Changes the vector potential without transforming canonical momentum.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing $\mathbf A$ without the canonical momentum shift changes the mechanical momentum artificially.

problems.flawedProof: Gauge transformations physically accelerate the particle because they change $\mathbf p$.

problems.title: Gauge change as a time-dependent canonical transformation
problems.objective: Realize electromagnetic gauge change as a time-dependent canonical transformation with unambiguous old and new momentum variables.
problems.statement: Let $F_2(\mathbf r,\mathbf P,t)=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf P-e\chi(\mathbf r,t)$. Derive the canonical map and new Hamiltonian. Show directly that it implements $\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$, $\Phi'=\Phi-\partial_t\chi$ without changing mechanical momentum.
permittedResults: Use $\mathbf p=\nabla_{\mathbf r}F_2$ and $K=H+\partial_tF_2$.
problems.strategy: First: Declare old variables $(\mathbf r,\mathbf p)$ and new variables $(\mathbf Q,\mathbf P)$ before differentiating the generator. Next: Include the explicit time derivative and group the result into the primed potentials. Finally: Verify equality of the old and new mechanical momenta with the stated gauge signs.
hints: Declare old variables $(\mathbf r,\mathbf p)$ and new variables $(\mathbf Q,\mathbf P)$ before differentiating the generator.
Include the explicit time derivative and group the result into the primed potentials.
Verify equality of the old and new mechanical momenta with the stated gauge signs.
problems.solution:
$\mathbf Q=\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf p=\mathbf P-e
abla\chi$, hence $\mathbf P=\mathbf p+e
abla\chi$. Substitution into $H=(\mathbf p-e\mathbf A)^2/(2m)+e\Phi$ and addition of $-e\chi_t$ gives $K=[\mathbf P-e(\mathbf A+
abla\chi)]^2/(2m)+e(\Phi-\chi_t)$. Therefore $K=(\mathbf P-e\mathbf A')^2/(2m)+e\Phi'$ with exactly the stated primed potentials. Moreover $\mathbf P-e\mathbf A'=\mathbf p-e\mathbf A$, so mechanical momentum and the physical trajectory are unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Generator derivatives give $\mathbf P=\mathbf p+e\nabla\chi$ and unchanged position.
The explicit $-e\chi_t$ term transforms both vector and scalar potentials with the stated signs.
Equality $\mathbf P-e\mathbf A'=\mathbf p-e\mathbf A$ verifies physical momentum invariance.

commonErrors.description: Drops $e\partial_t\chi$ from the transformed Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: Omitting the generator's time derivative leaves the scalar potential untransformed and changes the electric field representation.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same symbols for old and new canonical momenta and creates a gauge-sign contradiction.
commonErrors.consequence: Conflating old and new momenta hides the sign direction of the gauge map and can falsely change mechanical momentum.

problems.flawedProof: After shifting momentum, set $K=H$ and omit $\partial_tF_2$. The vector potential changes by $\nabla\chi$ but the scalar potential remains $\Phi$, so the transformation is complete.

problems.title: Legendre-map failure at a singular velocity Hessian
problems.objective: Locate the exact boundary where a velocity Legendre map becomes singular without invoking machinery beyond regular Hamiltonian mechanics.
problems.statement: Consider $L(q,\dot q,t)=a\dot q^2/2+b(q,t)\dot q-V(q,t)$. Construct the Hamiltonian when $a\ne0$. Then set $a=0$ and prove why the same construction fails: identify the momentum relation and show velocity is undetermined by $(q,p,t)$. Do not introduce Dirac constraint theory.
permittedResults: Regularity is controlled by the velocity Hessian $a$, not by the presence of a velocity-linear term.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the velocity Hessian and momentum relation for general $a$. Next: Invert and transform only in the regular case. Finally: At $a=0$, display the momentum relation and the undetermined velocity explicitly.
hints: Compute the velocity Hessian and momentum relation for general $a$.
Invert and transform only in the regular case.
At $a=0$, display the momentum relation and the undetermined velocity explicitly.
problems.solution: For $a\ne0$, $p=a\dot q+b$, so $\dot q=(p-b)/a$ and $H=(p-b)^2/(2a)+V$. When $a=0$, the momentum equation reduces to $p=b(q,t)$ and contains no velocity. Thus many velocities share the same canonical data, and $p\dot q-L=[p-b]\dot q+V$ cannot become a unique function on unconstrained $(q,p)$ phase space. The boundary is failure of the ordinary Legendre transform, not proof that the Euler-Lagrange problem has no content.
rubricCriteria: For nonzero $a$, momentum is inverted and the Hamiltonian $(p-b)^2/(2a)+V$ follows.
At $a=0$, the relation $p=b(q,t)$ contains no velocity and cannot define an unconstrained phase-space Hamiltonian.
The conclusion is limited to failure of the ordinary Legendre construction, not failure of the variational dynamics.

commonErrors.description: Claims the velocity-linear term makes the Hessian nonzero.
commonErrors.consequence: A velocity-linear term contributes zero to the velocity Hessian and therefore cannot restore regularity.

commonErrors.description: Divides by $a$ after setting $a=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Dividing by a vanished quadratic coefficient is undefined and conceals the undetermined velocity.

problems.flawedProof: The velocity-linear term $b(q,t)\dot q$ makes the velocity Hessian equal to $b$, so the Legendre map remains invertible at $a=0$ whenever $b\ne0$.

problems.title: Hamiltonian in spherical coordinates
problems.objective: Carry the spherical kinetic metric through the Legendre transform and distinguish coordinate singularities from physical ones.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ has $L=m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi^2)/2-V(r,\theta,\phi)$. Derive all three canonical momenta and the Hamiltonian. State the coordinate singularity and identify a cyclic momentum when $V$ is independent of $\phi$.
permittedResults: Invert each momentum using its own metric factor.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the kinetic metric with respect to all three velocities. Next: Invert each relation and perform the full Legendre transform. Finally: Identify coordinate singularities and use azimuthal symmetry to find the conserved momentum.
hints: Differentiate the kinetic metric with respect to all three velocities.
Invert each relation and perform the full Legendre transform.
Identify coordinate singularities and use azimuthal symmetry to find the conserved momentum.
problems.solution: $p_r=m\dot r$, $p_\theta=mr^2\dot\theta$, and $p_\phi=mr^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi$. Therefore $H=p_r^2/(2m)+p_\theta^2/(2mr^2)+p_\phi^2/(2mr^2\sin^2\theta)+V$. The formula is coordinate-singular at $r=0$ and at $\sin\theta=0$, even when the underlying Cartesian mechanics is regular. If $V_\phi=0$, then $\dot p_\phi=-H_\phi=0$, so the azimuthal canonical momentum is conserved.
rubricCriteria: The three canonical momenta include $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\theta$ in their angular components.
Inversion yields the full Hamiltonian with reciprocal metric factors.
Azimuthal cyclicity conserves $p_\phi$, while $r=0$ and the polar axis are identified as chart singularities.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p_\theta=m\dot\theta$ and $p_\phi=m\dot\phi$.
commonErrors.consequence: Dropping spherical metric factors gives angular momenta with the wrong units and an incorrect kinetic energy.

commonErrors.description: Interprets polar-axis coordinate singularities as physical infinite energy for every trajectory.
commonErrors.consequence: A coordinate pole does not force a Cartesian trajectory to have infinite energy; regular states can cross with compatible momenta.

problems.flawedProof: The Hamiltonian is $(p_r^2+p_\theta^2+p_\phi^2)/(2m)+V$ because the basis vectors are unit vectors.

problems.title: Symplectic leapfrog map and its stability interval
problems.objective: Compose kick-drift-kick oscillator updates into one exact symplectic matrix and determine its full linear-stability interval.
problems.statement: For $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2q^2/2$, apply kick-drift-kick leapfrog with step $h$: $p_{n+1/2}=p_n-hm\omega^2q_n/2$, $q_{n+1}=q_n+hp_{n+1/2}/m$, and $p_{n+1}=p_{n+1/2}-hm\omega^2q_{n+1}/2$. Derive the one-step matrix, prove it is symplectic, and find the exact linear-stability interval.
permittedResults: In one canonical pair, determinant one is equivalent to the linear symplectic condition.
problems.strategy: First: Eliminate the half-step momentum to obtain one matrix in $(q,p)$. Next: Compute determinant and trace exactly. Finally: Use the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion to derive the stability interval.
hints: Eliminate the half-step momentum to obtain one matrix in $(q,p)$.
Compute determinant and trace exactly.
Use the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion to derive the stability interval.
problems.solution: Writing $x=h\omega$, the map is $\begin{pmatrix}q_{n+1}\\p_{n+1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1-x^2/2&h/m\\-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)&1-x^2/2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}q_n\\p_n\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $(1-x^2/2)^2+x^2(1-x^2/4)=1$, so it is symplectic. The trace is $2(1-x^2/2)$. Eigenvalues remain on the unit circle when $|1-x^2/2|\le1$, giving $0\le h\omega\le2$, with strict interior for nondegenerate stable oscillation. This is a map-stability condition, not a claim of exact physical frequency.
rubricCriteria: The half-step momentum is eliminated without replacing the second kick by an old-position force.
The resulting matrix has determinant one and trace $2(1-x^2/2)$.
The unit-circle criterion gives strict stability for $0<h\omega<2$ with both boundary cases distinguished.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the two kicks into one full kick at the old position.
commonErrors.consequence: Evaluating both kicks at the old coordinate changes the integrator and its matrix coefficients.

commonErrors.description: Calls determinant one sufficient for bounded motion without checking the trace.
commonErrors.consequence: Area preservation alone allows hyperbolic eigenvalues; trace is essential for bounded iteration.

problems.flawedProof: Combine the two half-kicks into one full kick evaluated at $q_n$, then drift. This gives the same symplectic map and proves stability for every step size.

problems.title: Explicit Euler versus symplectic Euler on an oscillator
problems.objective: Contrast explicit and symplectic Euler maps through determinant and physical-energy changes rather than method labels.
problems.statement: For the harmonic oscillator compare explicit Euler, $q'=q+hp/m$, $p'=p-hm\omega^2q$, with kick-drift symplectic Euler, $p'=p-hm\omega^2q$, $q'=q+hp'/m$. Derive both matrices, determinants, and one-step energy changes through leading nonzero order. Explain why determinant one does not mean exact energy conservation.
permittedResults: Keep the updated momentum inside the symplectic-Euler coordinate step.
problems.strategy: First: Construct both update matrices without mixing old and new variables. Next: Evaluate determinants and substitute updates into the quadratic energy. Finally: Separate exact energy conservation from area preservation and long-time bounded error.
hints: Construct both update matrices without mixing old and new variables.
Evaluate determinants and substitute updates into the quadratic energy.
Separate exact energy conservation from area preservation and long-time bounded error.
problems.solution: Explicit Euler has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&h/m\\-hm\omega^2&1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $1+h^2\omega^2>1$; direct substitution gives $H'-H=h^2[\omega^2p^2/(2m)+m\omega^4q^2/2]>0$. Symplectic Euler has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1-h^2\omega^2&h/m\\-hm\omega^2&1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant one. Direct expansion gives $H'-H=h^2[\omega^2p^2/(2m)-m\omega^4q^2/2]-h^3\omega^4pq+h^4m\omega^6q^2/2$, so its leading term is sign dependent and not identically zero. Its long-time error is bounded in the stable regime. Symplecticity preserves phase area and a nearby modified invariant, not the exact original energy at each step.
rubricCriteria: Each update order is translated into its correct two-by-two matrix.
Explicit Euler expands area and increases the oscillator energy by the stated positive $h^2$ term.
Symplectic Euler has determinant one but a sign-dependent energy defect, separating area preservation from exact energy conservation.

commonErrors.description: Claims explicit Euler preserves area because its trace is two.
commonErrors.consequence: Matrix trace does not equal determinant, so trace two cannot certify explicit Euler's phase area.

commonErrors.description: Claims every determinant-one map preserves the original Hamiltonian exactly.
commonErrors.consequence: A determinant-one map can preserve a nearby invariant while changing the original Hamiltonian at each step.

problems.flawedProof: Both update matrices have trace two, so both determinants equal one. Therefore explicit Euler and symplectic Euler preserve area and exactly conserve oscillator energy.

problems.title: Accelerating-frame canonical map with the required time term
problems.objective: Verify the held accelerating-frame generator including its explicit-time term, equations, conserved Hamiltonian, and numerical frame conversion.
problems.statement: A free particle has $H=p^2/(2m)$. Define $Q=q-at^2/2$ and $P=p-mat$. Verify the type-2 generator $F_2=(q-at^2/2)(P+mat)+ma^2t^3/6$, derive the transformed Hamiltonian, and recover the accelerating-frame equation. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $a=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $q(0)=0$, and $p(0)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, evaluate $(Q,P)$ and $K$ at $t=2.00$ s.
permittedResults: Use $K=H+\partial_tF_2$ at fixed $(q,P)$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the generator to verify both canonical relations. Next: Calculate the explicit time term before rewriting in new variables. Finally: Check transformed equations and the numerical conserved Hamiltonian against inertial motion.
hints: Differentiate the generator to verify both canonical relations.
Calculate the explicit time term before rewriting in new variables.
Check transformed equations and the numerical conserved Hamiltonian against inertial motion.
problems.solution: $F_{2,q}=P+mat=p$ and $F_{2,P}=q-at^2/2=Q$. Substitution into $H+F_{2,t}$ yields $K=P^2/(2m)+maQ$. Thus $\dot Q=P/m$, $\dot P=-ma$, and $\ddot Q=-a$, while $q=Q+at^2/2$ gives $\ddot q=0$. At $t=2$ s, inertial motion has $q=8.00$ m and $p=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so $Q=2.00$ m and $P=-4.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Then $K=16/(4)+2(3)(2)=16.0$ J, equal to its initial value. Dropping $F_{2,t}$ gives the wrong equations.
rubricCriteria: Both generator derivatives recover $Q=q-at^2/2$ and $p=P+mat$.
Adding $F_{2,t}$ reduces the Hamiltonian to $P^2/(2m)+maQ$ with the correct fictitious-force sign.
The numerical state gives $(Q,P)=(2,-4)$ and $K=16.0$ J at two times.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes $p=P+mat$ into $H$ but omits $F_{2,t}$.
commonErrors.consequence: Variable substitution without $F_{2,t}$ leaves spurious time dependence and fails the accelerating-frame equations.

commonErrors.description: Uses potential $-maQ$ and predicts $\ddot Q=+a$.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing the fictitious potential predicts acceleration with the frame rather than opposite to it.

problems.flawedProof: The transformed Hamiltonian is $(P+mat)^2/(2m)$, so it depends explicitly on time and is not conserved.

problems.title: Oscillator flow as a canonical phase rotation
problems.objective: Represent scaled oscillator evolution as a one-parameter symplectic rotation and identify its infinitesimal generator.
problems.statement: In scaled canonical variables let $H=\omega(P^2+Q^2)/2$. Solve the Hamiltonian flow and show it is a rotation through angle $\omega t$. Prove the rotation matrix is symplectic and identify its generator at $t=0$.
permittedResults: Hamilton's equations are $\dot Q=\omega P$ and $\dot P=-\omega Q$.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the coupled first-order equations as a matrix exponential. Next: Verify the symplectic identity and determinant. Finally: Differentiate at zero and compare with the Hamiltonian vector field generator.
hints: Solve the coupled first-order equations as a matrix exponential.
Verify the symplectic identity and determinant.
Differentiate at zero and compare with the Hamiltonian vector field generator.
problems.solution: The solution is $(Q(t),P(t))^{\mathsf T}=R(\omega t)(Q_0,P_0)^{\mathsf T}$ with $R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. It has determinant one and satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}JR=J$. Its derivative at zero is $\omega J$, matching the Hamiltonian vector field matrix. The radius $Q^2+P^2$ and hence $H$ are invariant. Reversing the sign of the lower-left entry would produce a hyperbolic, not rotational, flow.
rubricCriteria: Opposite Hamilton-equation signs lead to the rotation matrix $R(\omega t)$.
The matrix preserves both $J$ and the radius $Q^2+P^2$.
Differentiation at zero gives $\omega J$, consistent with the Hamiltonian vector field.

commonErrors.description: Uses equal signs in the two Hamilton equations and obtains exponential growth.
commonErrors.consequence: Equal signs turn the elliptic generator into a hyperbolic one and destroy the oscillator invariant.

commonErrors.description: Treats an orthogonal matrix with determinant negative one as a canonical rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: An orthogonal reflection has determinant minus one and reverses the canonical area orientation.

problems.flawedProof: Use equal signs in Hamilton's equations, $\dot Q=\omega P$ and $\dot P=+\omega Q$. The resulting exponential flow has phase angle $2\omega t$ because the Hamiltonian is quadratic.

problems.title: Ermakov invariant for a time-dependent oscillator
problems.objective: Prove the dimensional Ermakov invariant by coupling a physical time-dependent oscillator to a positive auxiliary amplitude.
problems.statement: Let $q$ solve $\ddot q+\omega(t)^2q=0$. Let a positive auxiliary amplitude $\rho$ solve $\ddot\rho+\omega(t)^2\rho=c^2/\rho^3$, where $c>0$ is constant. Prove that $I=\tfrac12[(cq/\rho)^2+(\rho\dot q-\dot\rho q)^2]$ is conserved. State the required regularity, dimensions, and why positivity of $\rho$ matters.
permittedResults: Differentiate the proposed invariant and use both differential equations.
Assume $q,\rho\in C^2$ and $\rho(t)>0$ on the interval of interest.
problems.strategy: First: Introduce two quadratures whose squared sum is the invariant. Next: Differentiate them and reduce the result using both evolution equations. Finally: Show exact cancellation, audit dimensions, and state the nonvanishing-amplitude domain.
hints: Introduce two quadratures whose squared sum is the invariant.
Differentiate them and reduce the result using both evolution equations.
Show exact cancellation, audit dimensions, and state the nonvanishing-amplitude domain.
problems.solution: Set $u=cq/\rho$ and $v=\rho\dot q-\dot\rho q$. Then $\dot u=cv/\rho^2$. The two equations give $\dot v=\rho\ddot q-\ddot\rho q=-c^2q/\rho^3=-cu/\rho^2$. Hence $\dot I=u\dot u+v\dot v=ucv/\rho^2-vcu/\rho^2=0$. If $q$ and $\rho$ have length units, then $c$ has units $\mathrm{m^2/s}$ and both $u$ and $v$ have units $\mathrm{m^2/s}$, so $I$ has units $\mathrm{m^4/s^2}$. Positivity prevents division by zero and selects a regular auxiliary branch; the proof applies on any interval where $\rho\ne0$.
rubricCriteria: The two quadratures $u=cq/\rho$ and $v=\rho\dot q-\dot\rho q$ are differentiated exactly.
Both evolution equations give reciprocal rotations $\dot u=cv/\rho^2$ and $\dot v=-cu/\rho^2$.
Conservation, dimensions, regularity, and the nonvanishing domain of $\rho$ are all stated.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the physical oscillator equation and never invokes the auxiliary Ermakov equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The cancellation depends on the nonlinear auxiliary equation; the physical oscillator equation alone leaves uncancelled terms.

commonErrors.description: Divides by $\rho$ without requiring a nonzero auxiliary solution.
commonErrors.consequence: A zero of $\rho$ makes both the invariant expression and its derivative proof singular.

problems.flawedProof: Differentiate $I$ using only $\ddot q+\omega(t)^2q=0$ and never use the auxiliary equation for $\rho$. The remaining terms vanish automatically, so every positive $\rho$ produces an invariant.

problems.title: Synthesis and stability of two canonical shears
problems.objective: Synthesize two canonical shears in a declared order and classify repeated-map stability from the composite trace.
problems.statement: Compose the coordinate shear $A:(q,p)\mapsto(q+ap,p)$ with the momentum shear $B:(Q_1,P_1)\mapsto(Q_1,P_1-bQ_1)$, where $a,b$ are real constants with reciprocal units. Derive the composite matrix $M$, prove it is canonical, give type-2 generators for both stages, and classify the linear stability of repeated application of $M$.
permittedResults: A type-2 generator for the first stage is $F_2(q,P_1)=qP_1+aP_1^2/2$.
For a real two-by-two unit-determinant matrix, elliptic stability requires $|\operatorname{tr}M|<2$.
problems.strategy: First: Write and multiply the two shear matrices in the stated order. Next: Derive each stage from its type-2 generator and verify unit determinant. Finally: Use the trace criterion to classify all parameter regimes, including marginal boundaries.
hints: Write and multiply the two shear matrices in the stated order.
Derive each stage from its type-2 generator and verify unit determinant.
Use the trace criterion to classify all parameter regimes, including marginal boundaries.
problems.solution: The matrices are $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-b&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $M=BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\-b&1-ab\end{pmatrix}$. Both factors and their product have determinant one, hence are symplectic in one canonical pair. The first stage follows from $F_2(q,P_1)=qP_1+aP_1^2/2$; the second follows from $G_2(Q_1,P)=Q_1P+bQ_1^2/2$, which gives $P_1=P+bQ_1$. Since $\operatorname{tr}M=2-ab$, repeated motion is elliptic for $0<ab<4$, hyperbolic for $ab<0$ or $ab>4$, and marginal at $ab=0$ or $4$. The product $ab$ is dimensionless, as the trace requires.
rubricCriteria: Matrix multiplication gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\-b&1-ab\end{pmatrix}$ in the temporal order stated.
Separate type-2 generators reproduce the coordinate and momentum shears.
The trace criterion divides $ab$ into elliptic, hyperbolic, and marginal regimes with a dimensionless product.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the factors and silently analyzes $AB$ instead of the stated $BA$ map.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing factors changes the actual phase-space update even though some spectral invariants happen to agree.

commonErrors.description: Calls every determinant-one map stable without testing its trace.
commonErrors.consequence: Unit determinant guarantees symplectic area, not bounded powers of the map.

problems.flawedProof: Apply the leftmost shear first and use $M=AB=\begin{pmatrix}1-ab&a\\-b&1\end{pmatrix}$ for the stated map. This is the requested composite because matrix order does not matter for canonical shears.

problems.title: Mass-metric symplectic diagonalization of quadratic motion
problems.objective: Mass-normalize a positive quadratic Hamiltonian through a generalized eigenbasis while preserving the canonical one-form.
problems.statement: Let $H=\tfrac12\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}\mathbf p+\tfrac12\mathbf q^{\mathsf T}K\mathbf q$, where $M$ and $K$ are real symmetric positive-definite $n\times n$ matrices. Suppose columns of $V$ solve $KV=MV\Omega^2$ and are normalized by $V^{\mathsf T}MV=\mathbf1$. Prove that $\mathbf q=V\mathbf Q$, $\mathbf p=MV\mathbf P$ is canonical and reduces $H$ to independent oscillators. Apply the result to $M=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ and $K=\operatorname{diag}(8,9)$.
permittedResults: Use preservation of the canonical one-form: $\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}d\mathbf q=\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}d\mathbf Q$.
Positive definiteness guarantees positive generalized eigenvalues and an $M$-orthonormal eigenbasis.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the generalized eigenproblem with the mass-weighted normalization. Next: Check the canonical one-form before substituting into both quadratic forms. Finally: Evaluate the numerical matrices and verify the two decoupled frequencies.
hints: Solve the generalized eigenproblem with the mass-weighted normalization.
Check the canonical one-form before substituting into both quadratic forms.
Evaluate the numerical matrices and verify the two decoupled frequencies.
problems.solution: Because $V^{\mathsf T}MV=\mathbf1$, the proposed map gives $\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}d\mathbf q=\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}V^{\mathsf T}MVd\mathbf Q=\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}d\mathbf Q$, so it is canonical. Substitution yields $H=\tfrac12\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}\mathbf P+\tfrac12\mathbf Q^{\mathsf T}(V^{\mathsf T}KV)\mathbf Q=\sum_i(P_i^2+\omega_i^2Q_i^2)/2$. For the example, $\Omega^2=\operatorname{diag}(4,9)$ and $V=\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt2,1)$. Thus $q_1=Q_1/\sqrt2$, $q_2=Q_2$, $p_1=\sqrt2P_1$, $p_2=P_2$, and the frequencies are $2$ and $3$ in the supplied units. Each product $P_i\,dQ_i$ retains action units even though mass normalization changes the separate coordinate and momentum units.
rubricCriteria: Generalized eigenvectors satisfy $KV=MV\Omega^2$ and $V^{\mathsf T}MV=\mathbf1$.
The paired transformations $\mathbf q=V\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf p=MV\mathbf P$ preserve $\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}d\mathbf q$.
The numerical matrices yield independent frequencies two and three with consistent mass-normalized action units.

commonErrors.description: Transforms coordinates by $V$ but transforms momenta by the same $V$ without checking the one-form.
commonErrors.consequence: Using $V$ on momentum as well as coordinate is canonical only for Euclidean-orthogonal $V$, not a general mass metric.

commonErrors.description: Diagonalizes $K$ alone and ignores a nontrivial mass metric.
commonErrors.consequence: Diagonalizing stiffness without mass weighting gives the wrong modes whenever $M$ is not proportional to identity.

problems.flawedProof: Use $\mathbf q=V\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf p=V\mathbf P$. Applying the same matrix to coordinates and momenta is automatically canonical, so checking the canonical one-form is unnecessary.

problems.title: Fundamental solutions build a time-dependent oscillator invariant
problems.objective: Construct canonical linear invariants for a genuinely time-dependent oscillator from normalized fundamental solutions and distinguish their quadratic invariant from instantaneous energy.
problems.statement: Let $H(q,p,t)=p^2/(2m)+m\omega(t)^2q^2/2$, and let $u,v$ solve $\ddot x+\omega(t)^2x=0$ with $u(0)=1$, $\dot u(0)=0$, $v(0)=0$, and $\dot v(0)=1$. Prove that their Wronskian is one, derive two linear invariants that recover $(q_0,p_0)$, prove that their map is canonical, and build a quadratic invariant equal to the initial oscillator energy. Then take $\tau>0$ and $\omega(t)^2=2/(t+\tau)^2$ on the interval $t>-\tau$. Derive the normalized $u,v$ and, for $\tau=1.00\,\mathrm s$, $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $t=\tau$, $q=0.400\,\mathrm m$, and $p=-0.600\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, evaluate the basis functions, both linear invariants, the quadratic invariant, the instantaneous energy, and $\dot H$.
permittedResults: For any two solutions of $\ddot x+\omega(t)^2x=0$, Abel's identity makes their Wronskian constant.
For $\omega(t)^2=2/(t+\tau)^2$, set $s=1+t/\tau$ and try powers $s^r$.
problems.strategy: First: Invert the fundamental-solution matrix to express initial data as time-independent linear combinations of current phase-space variables. Next: verify the Poisson bracket and use those invariants to form the initial-energy quadratic. Finally: solve the Euler equation for the supplied frequency and compare the invariant numerically with the explicitly time-dependent Hamiltonian.
hints: Differentiate $A=\dot vq-vp/m$ and $B=up-m\dot uq$ using Hamilton's equations.
Check canonicity by evaluating $\{A,B\}=u\dot v-v\dot u$.
For the explicit frequency, the Euler exponents are $(1\pm i\sqrt7)/2$; impose all four initial conditions before evaluating.
problems.solution: The normalized Wronskian is $W=u\dot v-\dot uv=1$. Hamilton's equations show that $A=\dot vq-vp/m=q_0$ and $B=up-m\dot uq=p_0$ have zero total time derivative. Moreover $\{A,B\}=u\dot v-v\dot u=1$, so $(A,B)$ is a canonical pair. Therefore $I=B^2/(2m)+m\omega(0)^2A^2/2$ is invariant and equals the initial energy, although $H(q,p,t)$ need not be. On the declared domain, $s=1+t/\tau>0$; with $a=\sqrt7/2$, the normalized solutions are $u=\sqrt s[\cos(a\ln s)-\sin(a\ln s)/\sqrt7]$ and $v=(2\tau/\sqrt7)\sqrt s\sin(a\ln s)$. At $s=2$ they give $u=0.435913$, $v=0.848553\,\mathrm s$, $\dot u=-0.848553\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\dot v=0.642233$, with $W=1.00000$. Thus $A=0.511459\,\mathrm m$ and $B=0.417295\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Since $\omega(0)^2=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $I=0.566715\,\mathrm J$. At the same event $\omega^2=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so $H=0.170000\,\mathrm J$. Finally $\dot H=\partial H/\partial t=[m\,d(\omega^2)/dt]q^2/2=-0.0800\,\mathrm W$, explicitly confirming that the invariant is not instantaneous energy.
rubricCriteria: The Wronskian-one inverse gives $A=\dot vq-vp/m$ and $B=up-m\dot uq$, and direct differentiation proves both are invariant.
The Poisson bracket is one, the Euler-equation basis satisfies all four initial conditions, and $I=B^2/(2m)+m\omega(0)^2A^2/2$ is distinguished from $H(t)$.
The numerical basis, $A$, $B$, $I=0.566715$ J, $H=0.170000$ J, and $\dot H=-0.0800$ W are mutually consistent.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the oscillator energy $H$ is conserved merely because no damping appears.
commonErrors.consequence: Explicit time dependence in $\omega(t)$ does work at rate $\partial H/\partial t$, so this misses both the nonzero power and the actual invariant.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the fundamental matrix with plus signs or omits the mass factors in $A$ and $B$.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting combinations fail the derivative test, the Wronskian check, or the canonical Poisson bracket.

problems.flawedProof: There is no damping, so $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega(t)^2q^2/2$ must be constant. Therefore the fundamental solutions are unnecessary and the requested invariant is simply the instantaneous Hamiltonian.

problems.title: Jacobi constant from the rotating three-body Hamiltonian
problems.objective: Recover the circular restricted three-body Jacobi constant from its autonomous rotating Hamiltonian and explicit normalization.
problems.statement: In normalized planar circular restricted three-body coordinates, put primaries at $(-\mu,0)$ and $(1-\mu,0)$, define $r_1^2=(x+\mu)^2+y^2$ and $r_2^2=(x-1+\mu)^2+y^2$, and let $U=(1-\mu)/r_1+\mu/r_2$. Starting from $H=(p_x^2+p_y^2)/2+yp_x-xp_y-U$, derive the velocity-momentum relations and prove $C=-2H=x^2+y^2+2U-(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)$ is conserved away from collisions. State every normalization and the reason inertial energy need not be conserved.
permittedResults: Hamilton's equations give $\dot x=p_x+y$ and $\dot y=p_y-x$.
The normalized total mass, primary separation, gravitational constant times total mass, and rotation rate are all one.
problems.strategy: First: Derive and invert the two coordinate Hamilton equations. Next: Substitute momenta into the autonomous Hamiltonian and simplify all rotation cross terms. Finally: Identify the collision domain, normalization, and distinction from inertial particle energy.
hints: Derive and invert the two coordinate Hamilton equations.
Substitute momenta into the autonomous Hamiltonian and simplify all rotation cross terms.
Identify the collision domain, normalization, and distinction from inertial particle energy.
problems.solution: The coordinate equations invert to $p_x=\dot x-y$ and $p_y=\dot y+x$. Substitution into the Hamiltonian gives $H=[\dot x^2+\dot y^2-x^2-y^2]/2-U$, hence $C=-2H=x^2+y^2+2U-(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)$. The rotating Hamiltonian is autonomous, so $dH/dt=0$ and $C$ is conserved wherever $r_1r_2\ne0$. The formula uses unit primary separation, unit rotation rate, and unit $G(m_1+m_2)$ with masses $1-\mu$ and $\mu$. In inertial coordinates the test particle sees moving primaries, so its mechanical energy alone need not be constant even though the rotating-frame Jacobi integral is.
rubricCriteria: Hamilton's coordinate equations give $p_x=\dot x-y$ and $p_y=\dot y+x$.
Substitution produces $C=x^2+y^2+2U-v^2$ with all rotation terms accounted for.
Autonomy, collision exclusions, normalized units, and the distinction from inertial particle energy are stated.

commonErrors.description: Sets canonical momenta equal to rotating-frame velocities and loses both Coriolis terms.
commonErrors.consequence: Equating rotating canonical momenta with velocities removes coordinate shifts and loses the centrifugal contribution.

commonErrors.description: Calls $C$ an inertial mechanical energy without accounting for the rotating coordinates.
commonErrors.consequence: The Jacobi integral belongs to the rotating autonomous system and is not the test particle's inertial mechanical energy.

problems.flawedProof: Set $p_x=\dot x$ and $p_y=\dot y$ in the rotating frame. Then $C=2U-(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)$ because the Coriolis coupling never affects momentum.

problems.title: Axial dynamics in an axisymmetric magnetic bottle
problems.objective: Construct the cylindrical Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric magnetic bottle and derive its signed axial canonical force.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ and signed charge $e$ moves with zero scalar potential in the axisymmetric vector potential $\mathbf A=A_\phi\mathbf e_\phi$, where $A_\phi=B_0(1+\alpha z^2)r/2$ and $\alpha\ge0$. Derive the cylindrical Hamiltonian, prove $p_\phi$ is conserved, compute $\mathbf B$, and derive the exact axial canonical force $\dot p_z$. Check the uniform-field limit $\alpha\to0$ and state the units of $\alpha$.
permittedResults: In cylindrical coordinates, $p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi+erA_\phi$.
For an azimuthal vector potential, $B_r=-\partial_zA_\phi$ and $B_z=r^{-1}\partial_r(rA_\phi)$.
problems.strategy: First: Construct canonical momenta from the cylindrical velocity metric and vector-potential coupling. Next: Take the curl and use axisymmetry before differentiating the reduced Hamiltonian. Finally: Derive the signed axial force and check its dimensions and uniform-field limit.
hints: Construct canonical momenta from the cylindrical velocity metric and vector-potential coupling.
Take the curl and use axisymmetry before differentiating the reduced Hamiltonian.
Derive the signed axial force and check its dimensions and uniform-field limit.
problems.solution: Writing $S=p_\phi-erA_\phi$, the Hamiltonian is $H=(p_r^2+p_z^2)/(2m)+S^2/(2mr^2)$. Axisymmetry gives $\dot p_\phi=0$. The curl is $\mathbf B=-B_0\alpha zr\,\mathbf e_r+B_0(1+\alpha z^2)\,\mathbf e_z$. Since $\partial_zS=-eB_0\alpha zr^2$, Hamilton's equation gives $\dot p_z=-\partial_zH=eB_0\alpha zS/m$. Here $S=mr^2\dot\phi$ is the mechanical axial angular momentum; the sign of the axial force therefore depends on signed charge and instantaneous azimuthal motion. The parameter $\alpha$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. At $\alpha=0$, $\mathbf B=B_0\mathbf e_z$ and $\dot p_z=0$.
rubricCriteria: The canonical azimuthal momentum includes $mr^2\dot\phi+erA_\phi$ and is conserved by symmetry.
Taking the curl gives both radial and axial magnetic-field components with zero-divergence-compatible signs.
Differentiation yields $\dot p_z=eB_0\alpha zS/m$ with units and the uniform-field limit checked.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p_\phi=mr\dot\phi+eA_\phi$ and misses both cylindrical factors.
commonErrors.consequence: Missing cylindrical factors changes canonical angular momentum dimensions and the effective azimuthal energy.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the force must always point toward $z=0$ without retaining the signed mechanical angular momentum.
commonErrors.consequence: The axial-force direction depends on signed charge and mechanical angular momentum, so it cannot be fixed inward universally.

problems.flawedProof: Use $p_\phi=mr\dot\phi+eA_\phi$, omitting one factor of $r$ from each term. The Hamiltonian is therefore $(p_\phi-eA_\phi)^2/(2mr)$ plus the radial and axial kinetic terms.

problems.title: Euler-angle Hamiltonian of a heavy symmetric top
problems.objective: Legendre-transform the heavy symmetric top in Euler angles and isolate its two cyclic momenta and polar chart boundary.
problems.statement: A symmetric top fixed at one point has transverse moment $I_1$, axial moment $I_3$, and Euler kinetic energy $T=I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)/2+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2/2$. The center of mass is distance $\ell$ along the body axis, $\theta$ is measured from the upward vertical, and $V=Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Derive all canonical momenta and the Hamiltonian. Identify the two conserved momenta and the coordinate-singular set.
permittedResults: First use $p_\psi$ to eliminate the repeated combination $\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta$.
The angles $\phi$ and $\psi$ are cyclic for the stated axisymmetric gravitational model.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the full kinetic energy with respect to all three Euler rates. Next: Invert the coupled $\phi$ and $\psi$ momentum relations before taking the Legendre transform. Finally: Use cyclicity to identify constants and interpret the polar coordinate singularity.
hints: Differentiate the full kinetic energy with respect to all three Euler rates.
Invert the coupled $\phi$ and $\psi$ momentum relations before taking the Legendre transform.
Use cyclicity to identify constants and interpret the polar coordinate singularity.
problems.solution: $p_\theta=I_1\dot\theta$, $p_\psi=I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)$, and $p_\phi=I_1\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+p_\psi\cos\theta$. Thus $\dot\phi=(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)/(I_1\sin^2\theta)$ and $\dot\psi=p_\psi/I_3-\dot\phi\cos\theta$. The Legendre transform is $H=p_\theta^2/(2I_1)+(p_\phi-p_\psi\cos\theta)^2/(2I_1\sin^2\theta)+p_\psi^2/(2I_3)+Mg\ell\cos\theta$. Since $H$ is independent of $\phi$ and $\psi$, both $p_\phi$ and $p_\psi$ are conserved. The apparent singularity at $\sin\theta=0$ is an Euler-coordinate singularity; regular physical states there require the numerator to approach zero consistently.
rubricCriteria: All three momenta follow from the coupled kinetic metric, including the shared $\dot\phi$-$\dot\psi$ combination.
Rate inversion produces the standard Hamiltonian with the squared momentum difference over $\sin^2\theta$.
Only $p_\phi$ and $p_\psi$ are conserved, and regular polar states satisfy the numerator compatibility condition.

commonErrors.description: Treats all three Euler-angle momenta as independent scalar moments times their own rates.
commonErrors.consequence: Treating Euler rates as orthogonal ignores their kinetic coupling and yields an incorrect diagonal Hamiltonian.

commonErrors.description: Calls $p_\theta$ conserved even though gravity makes $\theta$ noncyclic.
commonErrors.consequence: Gravity and the kinetic metric depend on tilt, so $p_\theta$ is not a cyclic constant.

problems.flawedProof: The top Hamiltonian is the sum of three uncoupled terms $p_i^2/(2I_i)$ because Euler angles are orthogonal coordinates.

problems.title: Exact shadow Hamiltonian of oscillator leapfrog
problems.objective: Find the exact autonomous quadratic shadow Hamiltonian whose time-step flow equals stable oscillator leapfrog.
problems.statement: For the kick-drift-kick oscillator map of CM:227, write $x=h\omega$ and assume $0<x<2$. With $\theta=\arccos(1-x^2/2)$, construct an autonomous quadratic Hamiltonian whose exact time-$h$ flow is exactly one leapfrog step. Prove the match and expand the shadow Hamiltonian through order $h^2$. Audit the limits $h\to0$ and $x\to2^-$.
permittedResults: The leapfrog matrix has off-diagonal entries $h/m$ and $-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)$.
For $H_*=(\alpha p^2+\beta q^2)/2$, the flow angle is $h\sqrt{\alpha\beta}$.
problems.strategy: First: Express the stable symplectic matrix as the flow of a general diagonal quadratic Hamiltonian. Next: Solve its two coefficients from the exact off-diagonal matrix entries. Finally: Expand both coefficient factors and inspect the small-step and stability-boundary limits.
hints: Express the stable symplectic matrix as the flow of a general diagonal quadratic Hamiltonian.
Solve its two coefficients from the exact off-diagonal matrix entries.
Expand both coefficient factors and inspect the small-step and stability-boundary limits.
problems.solution: Because $\sin\theta=x\sqrt{1-x^2/4}$, define $H_{sh}=(\theta/\sin\theta)[p^2/(2m)+m\omega^2(1-x^2/4)q^2/2]$. Its frequency is $\sqrt{\alpha\beta}=\theta/h$. The exact time-$h$ flow therefore has diagonal entries $\cos\theta=1-x^2/2$, upper-right entry $(\alpha h/\theta)\sin\theta=h/m$, and lower-left entry $-(\beta h/\theta)\sin\theta=-hm\omega^2(1-x^2/4)$, exactly the leapfrog matrix. Since $\theta/\sin\theta=1+x^2/6+O(x^4)$, $H_{sh}=H+h^2[\omega^2p^2/(12m)-m\omega^4q^2/24]+O(h^4)$. It tends to $H$ as $h\to0$ but becomes singular as $x\to2^-$, matching the stability boundary.
rubricCriteria: The stable map angle satisfies $\cos\theta=1-x^2/2$ and determines both shadow coefficients.
Exact flow entries reproduce the leapfrog diagonal and both off-diagonal terms.
The $h^2$ expansion has the stated kinetic and potential corrections and becomes singular at the stability boundary.

problems.title: Stability chart for a kicked canonical oscillator
problems.objective: Build the ordered Floquet map of a kicked canonical oscillator and extract its exact stability chart from the trace.
problems.statement: In scaled canonical variables, free oscillator evolution through angle $\vartheta$ is $R=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\vartheta&\sin\vartheta\\-\sin\vartheta&\cos\vartheta\end{pmatrix}$. It is followed by an impulsive quadratic kick $P^+=P^- -\kappa Q$. Derive the stroboscopic matrix, prove it is symplectic, and obtain the exact bounded-stability condition. Specialize to $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and classify the boundaries.
permittedResults: The kick matrix is $K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\kappa&1\end{pmatrix}$ and the stated ordering is $M=KR$.
For determinant one, strict elliptic stability is $|\operatorname{tr}M|<2$.
problems.strategy: First: Translate the impulse and free evolution into matrices in the declared temporal order. Next: Multiply them, verify determinant one, and compute the trace. Finally: Apply the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion and inspect the quarter-period boundaries.
hints: Translate the impulse and free evolution into matrices in the declared temporal order.
Multiply them, verify determinant one, and compute the trace.
Apply the unit-determinant eigenvalue criterion and inspect the quarter-period boundaries.
problems.solution: Multiplication gives $M=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\kappa c-s&c-\kappa s\end{pmatrix}$, where $c=\cos\vartheta$ and $s=\sin\vartheta$. Both $K$ and $R$ have determinant one, so $M$ is symplectic. Its trace is $2c-\kappa s$, and repeated stroboscopic motion is elliptic precisely when $|2\cos\vartheta-\kappa\sin\vartheta|<2$. It is hyperbolic when the magnitude exceeds two and marginal at equality. For $\vartheta=\pi/2$, the condition is $|\kappa|<2$, with parabolic boundaries at $\kappa=\pm2$ unless the matrix degenerates to $\pm\mathbf1$, which it does not here.
rubricCriteria: Free rotation followed by kick is represented as $M=KR$ with the correct lower row.
Determinant one verifies symplecticity and trace $2\cos\vartheta-\kappa\sin\vartheta$ controls eigenvalues.
At a quarter period the stable band is $|\kappa|<2$ with nontrivial parabolic boundaries.

commonErrors.description: Uses $RK$ while claiming to apply the free evolution before the kick.
commonErrors.consequence: Using $RK$ applies the kick at the wrong phase and changes the stroboscopic coordinates.

commonErrors.description: Tests only determinant one and concludes every kick strength is bounded.
commonErrors.consequence: Symplectic kicked maps can be hyperbolic, so determinant alone cannot bound repeated motion.

problems.flawedProof: Although free evolution occurs before the kick, multiply in the opposite order and use $M=RK$. This is valid because both factors are symplectic, so their temporal order cannot affect the stroboscopic map.

problems.title: Freely falling canonical frame for a constant force
problems.objective: Construct a freely falling canonical frame that removes a uniform force exactly and verify the cancellation numerically.
problems.statement: A particle has $H=p^2/(2m)-Fq$ with constants $m>0$ and $F$, and put $a=F/m$. Construct a type-2 generator that implements $Q=q-at^2/2$ and $P=p-mat$ while reducing the new Hamiltonian exactly to $K=P^2/(2m)$. Verify every time-dependent term. Then for $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $F=6.00\,\mathrm N$, $q(0)=0$, and $p(0)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, find $(q,p,Q,P,K)$ at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$.
permittedResults: Try $F_2=(q-at^2/2)(P+mat)+g(t)$ and determine $g$ by cancellation.
For the original constant force, $p(t)=p_0+Ft$ and $q(t)=q_0+p_0t/m+at^2/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the generator to recover both requested canonical variables. Next: Compute its explicit time derivative at fixed old coordinate and new momentum, then cancel every force term. Finally: Evaluate the inertial and transformed trajectories numerically with units and verify constant $K$.
hints: Differentiate the generator to recover both requested canonical variables.
Compute its explicit time derivative at fixed old coordinate and new momentum, then cancel every force term.
Evaluate the inertial and transformed trajectories numerically with units and verify constant $K$.
problems.solution: Take $F_2(q,P,t)=(q-at^2/2)(P+mat)+ma^2t^3/3$. Then $p=F_{2,q}=P+mat$ and $Q=F_{2,P}=q-at^2/2$. At fixed $(q,P)$, $F_{2,t}=-atP+maq-3ma^2t^2/2+ma^2t^2$. Adding this to $(P+mat)^2/(2m)-maq$ cancels the terms in $atP$, $maq$, and $ma^2t^2$, leaving $K=P^2/(2m)$. Numerically $a=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; at $t=2.00$ s, $p=20.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $q=14.0$ m, so $P=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, $Q=8.00$ m, and $K=16.0$ J. The transformed free motion has constant $P$ and $\ddot Q=0$.
rubricCriteria: The generator produces both $Q=q-at^2/2$ and the essential momentum shift $P=p-mat$.
Its cubic time term cancels every residual force and leaves $K=P^2/(2m)$.
The computed inertial state maps to $(Q,P)=(8,8)$ and constant $K=16.0$ J.
